36. EVERY COMBAT SECTION CARRIES AN AFFIRMATIVE RUNG. A section that is 100% prohibitions
    after an edit is a defect regardless of token count: deck162 attacked in 2 of 6 attack
    windows and, on a board where the render said its attacker survives, wrote 300 words
    inventing a trade the tag had already ruled out. Name the rendered string that means
    GO ("(you kill it, your attacker lives)" -> SEND). Stops are cheap to write and cheap
    to over-apply; the positive branch is what bounds them. A rendered outcome vocabulary
    needs full coverage, not just its dangerous half.

37. A MULTI-ASK SEQUENCE IS ONE GOVERNED WINDOW. mulligan -> keep -> bottom, and
    cast -> target -> mode -> announce X, are single decisions split across asks. deck162's
    Rule 3 ("Cast Shield Sphere {0} ... take it every single time it is listed", 5/5) and
    its MULLIGAN section, which ends at the keep, never met — so it bottomed the Shield
    Sphere. Neither rule was violated. Each section says what happens at every ask in its
    sequence, or hands the next ask to another section BY NAME.

38. A MULLIGAN FLOOR IS AN IMPERATIVE, AND FLOOR-VS-BEHAVIOUR DIVERGENCE IS AN OWNER
    QUESTION. Fair hands make these seams testable for the first time. Write the floor as
    a step the executor performs and stops on ("count the lands on the header line; if 2
    or more, answer KEEP and read no further"), not as a declarative fact about which
    hands are keepable — deck146's guide says in terms that a one-land hand "is NOT on
    [the mulligan list] and is a KEEP" and the model mulliganed a one-land seven anyway
    (and won); deck125 mulliganed a 2-land hand its own floor keeps (and won the 52-turn
    game). n=1 in the model's favour is not evidence: never move a floor from a single
    window, never patch a floor in prose to match observed behaviour. Route the floor
    question to the owner with the hand, the render's own header numbers, and the outcome.

39. TOKENS AND CARDS ARE DIFFERENT NOUNS IN A COMBAT STOP. deck146's per-creature STOP was
    written about "a creature": it was right about CARDS (152's vigilant Tracker died to
    the violation) and wrong about TOKENS (146 vs123 seq 20 sent a token into the stop so
    the block was spent on the free body, and three real cards connected 11 -> 1 — the
    violation beat the rule). Combat prohibitions say CARD or TOKEN explicitly; the cost
    side of a stop differs by an order of magnitude between them.

40. A REPEATABLE ACTIVATION NEEDS AN ALREADY-ON CHECK POINTED AT A RENDERED FIELD.
    deck146 paid {3}{B} to animate a Hive of the Eye Tyrant 23 times in one game, 12 of
    them redundant (twice in one upkeep on turns 16/18/20/22/30/34/36/40, four times on
    44 and 46), while the battlefield line already read `Hive of the Eye Tyrant #1 (3/3)
    [menace]` and the header said "of which 1 is a creature". Two Silverquill Commands sat
    uncast in hand throughout. One line, cheaper than a mana-budget rule and verifiable
    from the transcript: "find it on your battlefield line; if it already reads (3/3),
    pass."

41. BUFF PLACEMENT ASKS A CONNECTION QUESTION BEFORE A SIZE QUESTION. Eight consecutive
    +1/+1 counters went onto one Luminarch Aspirant (2/2 -> 10/10) whose every attack tag
    read `Fog Bank (0/2) (neither dies (no combat damage is dealt either way -
    prevented))`; the 10/10 dealt zero and deck152 lost. Any recurring "choose a target
    for your own buff" rule must first ask whether that body's tag got through last
    combat. A buff-placement rule that mentions only stats is incomplete.

42. "NEITHER HALF DOES ANYTHING ALONE" IS A SYMMETRY CLAIM, AND COMBO HALVES ARE RARELY
    SYMMETRIC. Two of deck126's four wins had NO Exquisite Blood on the battlefield at any
    point (turn 15 with two Sanguine Bonds: 12 off the opponent in one combat; turn 26
    with one), while Exquisite Blood sat alone for 29 turns against a creatureless deck
    and never triggered. The asymmetry is derivable: Sanguine Bond consumes a resource the
    deck manufactures (life, from 16 defenders); Blood consumes one only the opponent can
    manufacture. For each half alone, ask whether the DECK's own engine already produces
    the input that half consumes. If it does, that half is a standalone plan and is taught
    as one, with the pair taught as the accelerated version.

43. A COLOUR OR MANA-SOURCE CLAIM IS A CARD FACT, NOT DECK LORE. deck126's guide asserted
    "your Bayous, Scrublands, Savannahs and Urborg already make black"; Savannah is
    `type=Land / subtype=Forest Plains` — {G}/{W} only. The claim gated a Chromatic Lantern
    entry and argued against the exact board on which the model correctly cast the Lantern.
    A wrong colour claim is invisible in playtest logs — the model simply follows a rule
    that is quietly against it — so it survives waves. Write every "these lands make X"
    statement from the primitives' `subtype=` / `auto={T}:Add` lines, card by card, and
    re-check it every wave the way card texts are re-checked.

44. ADJUDICATE A RENDER PREDICTION BY THE EMITTER'S ACTUAL STRING, NEVER BY THE LEDGER'S
    SHORTHAND NAME. The wave-44 Day/Night lane was reported FAIL 0/2035 by a sweep for a
    literal "Day/Night" token; the shipped emitter writes `It is currently Day.` /
    `It is currently Night.`, present in 236 records — a PASS. Before adjudicating a render
    lane, read the emitter in the code or a PARSETEST CHECK and search for the string it
    actually produces. This applies symmetrically to a PASS claimed off a shorthand grep.

45. UNDERPOWERED RATES ARE REPORTED DIRECTIONALLY, NEVER AS A RATE. The X-pricing
    behavioural prediction (">=60% cast at kills>=2 windows") had n=3: 2 of 3 = 67% clears
    the bar and one different decision makes it 33%. The loose metric (>=1 opponent kill)
    was 3 of 9 = 33%, identical to wave 43 — the render fix moved the strict metric only
    within noise. State the denominator with every rate; when n is small, report the
    direction and accumulate windows across corpora until the denominator can separate the
    hypotheses, or drop the numeric half and keep the render check. Do not close a lane on
    a low-power sample, and do not read one favourable sample as a discharge.

=====================================================================
EDITION AMENDMENTS — wave-45 (2026-08-26) — SECOND FAIR-HAND CORPUS
=====================================================================
Corpus `matchups-20260826-131833`, binary fd69fadc2, 1909 records / 1825 decisions,
2 fallbacks (0.11%), 8 mulligans, 21 games. Merge rule unchanged from wave 44: an
amendment ships on convergence across two or more seats, or on one decisive
falsification (a rule that cost a game, or a measured N-of-N obedience that ran the
wrong way). Numbering note: three seat files wrote against provisional "#46/#47"
odds-and-owner numbers that were never in the wave-44 edition; those proposals are
adjudicated here as 66 and 67, and no owner ruling exists or is implied — mulligan
and every other guide-content question is decided by the reviewers and this synthesis
from the corpus, because the owner does not design deck strategy.

46. EVERY DECISION KIND THE HARNESS CAN RAISE NEEDS A NAMED OWNER — AND THE FREE
    ACTION NEEDS ONE MOST. deck123's 278-line guide governed every priced decision
    and none of the free one: it answered "Play no land right now" thirteen
    consecutive times across seven of its own turns, frozen at two lands with three
    in hand, and lost 42-0 without ever casting its three-mana engine. deck125
    declined 14 of 81 turn-level drops and deck126 2 of 41, and the decline chains
    sit inside four losses across the two seats. All three guides mentioned the land
    drop only inside an opening "every turn is the same three actions" sentence.
    Before shipping a guide, enumerate the kinds the corpus itself labels — land
    drop, mulligan, bottoming, cast, target, mode, announce X, activation,
    attackers, blockers, forced sacrifice, reveal — and give each a named owner: a
    section, or one line in DECIDING SITUATIONS. A costless, always-correct action
    stated as scene-setting is an action the pilot skips whenever a plan sentence
    points elsewhere; "obvious" is a property of a reader who already knows the game.
    Extends #37 from a sequence to the whole ask space.

47. PRINT THE INTEGER BESIDE EVERY MANA SYMBOL A GUIDE NAMES. The executor read
    `{2}{u}` as two and re-emitted "Cast Intruder Alarm {2}{u} using Tundra and
    Underground Sea" in its plan for thirteen straight windows while the render said
    `Mana available: 2 total` each time; its own seq-25 reply reads "Actually, I have
    2 mana. I can cast Intruder Alarm now for {2}{u}. Wait, I ...". Wherever a guide
    names a cost, write the count next to the symbols — `Intruder Alarm {2}{u}
    (three mana)`, `{2}{b}{b} is FOUR` — in cast lists, curve tables and card lines
    alike. Amendment #33 made this ruling for the mana a rule RESERVES; it applies
    one layer down, to the cost of the card being cast.

48. ONE OPERATION ON ONE RENDERED FIELD; FOLD EVERY CORRECTION INTO THE CONSTANT.
    deck125's X ceiling asked for `7 - (handline - 1)`: read a field, subtract 1,
    subtract the result from 7. Obeyed 6/12. The identical rule as `8 - handline`
    reproduces all twelve verdicts with no intermediate value to lose. The wave-44
    edit that introduced the intermediate was right about the game and wrong about
    the executor — it made a correction VISIBLE as a step instead of folding it into
    the constant. If the arithmetic cannot be collapsed to one operation on one
    printed number, it is two rules and the second one will not fire. Keep the reason
    for the constant in one clause after the rule, where it explains without being a
    step.

49. GATE ON THE RENDERED TAG, NEVER ON A NUMERIC PROXY FOR IT. deck125's counter and
    sweeper sections gated on printed power ("power 0 or 1: let it resolve"; "cast
    the sweeper at printed power 4 or more") and leaked four counters and two
    sweepers onto Pride Guardian 0/3, Wall of Omens 0/4, Fog Bank 0/2 and Shield
    Sphere 0/6 — two of them the last answers in a game then lost to an uncountered
    Sanguine Bond. The Path section on the same seat names the `[defender]` TAG
    instead of a number and took 0 violations in 32 windows. deck126 lost a game to
    the same shape from the other side: its one removal spell was gated on a LIFE
    TOTAL (10 or less) when the fact that decided the game was `[flying]` on the
    opponent's only creature — a life threshold fires after the damage, the tag is
    visible before it. `[defender]` is a fact about what a creature can ever do;
    `printed power 0` is a fact about this instant. State the tag rule first and mark
    it as having no exception; the numeric rule then only has to cover what the tag
    does not.

50. A GATE AND A FORMULA THAT SIZE THE SAME ACTION SHARE ONE THRESHOLD, DERIVED FROM
    THE FORMULA. deck125 forbade casting Sphinx's Revelation "at hand 7 or more" and,
    four paragraphs later, gave a ceiling that permits X=1 at a hand line of 7. Two
    numbers for one boundary; the pilot cast at hand 7 and at hand 8, 6 of 12
    windows. Restating both at 8 removed the seam and changed no verdict. Two
    independently-stated thresholds for one boundary is a contradiction the executor
    resolves by whichever it read last.

51. WHEN A RULE GAINS AN EXCEPTION, EVERY LINE THAT SUMMARISES IT GAINS THE SAME
    EXCEPTION IN THE SAME EDIT — SECOND INSTANCE, NOW A DEFINITION-OF-DONE STEP.
    #24 established the quick-reference contract after deck130's face burn was
    authorised by a list line its own rule forbade. The same guide shipped a second
    instance in a different lane: rule #2 step 0 gained two named DO-NOT conditions
    in wave 44 and the closing line "Their board shows two or more creatures and
    Starstorm is in hand -> cast Starstorm" did not gain them. It has not cost a game
    only because the pilot happened to obey the rule instead of the list (5 windows,
    all correct). This is now mechanical: after editing a rule, grep the closing list
    for every line that restates it and edit them inside the same numbered edit, so a
    reviewer cannot ship half.

52. A NEWLY RENDERED STRING CREATES A SAME-WAVE OBLIGATION IN EVERY GUIDE THAT CAN
    SEE IT, AND A PROCEDURAL GATE WRITTEN OFF ONE SEAT GOES TO EVERY SEAT WITH THE
    SAME DECISION SURFACE. Wave-45's lane-A `GANG BLOCK:` clause priced deck152's
    fatal attack exactly and in advance ("their 6 biggest together deal 7, enough to
    kill this attacker"); deck152's guide has no rule keyed to the collapsed form or
    to the string, because in wave 44 only deck162 had seen it, so only deck162 got
    the teach. It cost a 7/7 Luminarch Aspirant, the seat's whole board, and the
    game, while the correct answer was on the screen. The mirror case: amendment
    #25's survival gate shipped to deck146 and deck152 in wave 44 and not to deck162,
    which has the same one-blocker-many-attackers exposure — its first live LETHAL
    window in wave 45 was its only loss's decisive decision (`B1:A2` survives at 1
    where blocking A1 survives at 4). Make both directions step deliverables: a lane
    that ships a rendered string names every guide in the pool that can see it and
    the seat reviewers answer "rule present / rule absent / not applicable" that
    wave; and this synthesis step enumerates, for every amendment written off one
    seat's evidence, which other guides share the decision surface, and either
    applies it or records why not. #32's cross-guide index is the register both use.

53. WHEN A CROSS-GUIDE TEACH FAILS AT EVERY SEAT, DIAGNOSE PER GUIDE FROM THE
    OVERRIDE ARGUMENT IN EACH REPLY — DO NOT REWORD IT ONCE. The per-creature STOP on
    the attack tag `(your attacker dies, their blocker lives)` was offered on a
    non-token CARD 7 times across deck146, deck152 and deck162 and violated 7 times;
    five of the seven cards died, and it is in the causal chain of three losses. The
    tempting conclusion is that the rule is unteachable. The replies say otherwise
    and say three different things: deck146 lost it to a competing EXCEPTION landing
    on the same rendered A-row (a Shield Sphere carve-out and the stop both applied
    and nothing said which won — the reply obeyed the exception by name); deck152
    lost it to a BENEFIT printed inside the stop's own parenthesis (see 55); deck162
    lost it to LIFE PRESSURE with no counter-argument written down (300 words of mana
    arithmetic that never engage the tag). A single canonical rewording would have
    fixed at most one. Read the three replies for three arguments before proposing
    one rule, and write each fix in the vocabulary of the argument that beat it there
    (#28). Companion, from the same evidence: an exception's scope is stated in terms
    of the rendered STRING, not the card ("the exception applies only when EVERY name
    on the tag is a Shield Sphere"), and every exception gets a Definition-of-Done
    check that constructs the tag where both fire and confirms the guide answers it.

54. OUTNUMBERING THEIR UNTAPPED BLOCKERS DOES NOT MAKE A SEND SAFE — THE DEFENDER
    CHOOSES WHICH ATTACKER TO BLOCK. Present in 4 of the 7 violations above, in three
    guides, each of which told the seat that a body count made the swing safe (146
    and 152 as a token carve-out, which the pilot generalised to cards). At deck152
    vs162 seq 20 there was ONE untapped blocker and TWO attackers, and the defender
    duly ate the Intrepid Adversary rather than the Wolf that would have killed it.
    Any rule that reduces a combat decision to comparing two counts states this in
    the same sentence: they pick the blocker, and they pick the one their block wins.
    Extends #29 from lifegain walls to the allocation itself.

55. A BENEFIT PRINTED INSIDE A FATAL PARENTHESIS IS INSTEAD OF, NOT AS WELL AS. On
    `(your attacker dies, their blocker lives (lifelink: you gain 3))` deck152 wrote,
    verbatim: "The Intrepid Adversaries gain 3 life each via lifelink (total +6 life)
    and deal 6 damage to the opponent (reducing them to 4)." Both cannot happen — the
    lifelink gain is what the blocked fight pays while the attacker dies; the face
    damage is what happens instead, if they decline. #30 found this with a keyword
    that REMOVES a stated cost (vigilance vs a tapping rationale); this is the
    complement, a keyword that ADDS a stated benefit inside the stop's own
    parentheses. For every stop keyed to a rendered outcome, list the keywords that
    can appear inside that outcome's brackets — lifelink, deathtouch, trample, first
    strike, infect — and state for each whether it changes the verdict, and where the
    keyword prints a number, say which branch that number belongs to. A parenthesis
    that mixes a bad outcome with a good number is the most reliable way to lose a
    rule.

56. #25 HAS AN ATTACK-SIDE TWIN: A FLOOR EVALUATES, IT NEVER ALLOCATES THE LAST BODY.
    #25 put a survival gate above the block ladder because a ladder ranks options and
    cannot answer "which attacker do I spend my one blocker on". deck130 lost a game
    to the mirror: its ATTACK FLOOR ranks bodies ("send everything except
    Blastminer"; "if their power totals your life, send only Rorix") and cannot
    answer "should my ONLY creature attack, when it is also my only blocker". At 4
    life against a vigilant 4/4, opponent on 15, the floor's own hold-back clause was
    TRUE and its instruction was still "send only Rorix" — 4 into 4 life beats 6 into
    15, and Rorix held home kills the 4/4 and lives, a trade the blockers screen
    prints. Every attack section for a deck that can be reduced to one creature
    carries a RACE gate above the floor, written as two divisions over rendered
    numbers (their turns to kill you / your turns to kill them), with vigilance named
    as the keyword that keeps an attacking creature on the defensive side of the sum.
    Label attack rules EVALUATION or SELECTION exactly as #25 requires for blocks.

57. TWO MENU PATHS THAT DISPOSE OF THE SAME CARD NEED A VERDICT EACH, BY THEIR
    RENDERED ROW NAMES — INCLUDING THE DEGENERATE PATH. deck130's guide has a whole
    opening rule about not cycling its spells and a correct release for the one board
    where cycling IS right. At exactly that board (opponent "of which 0 are
    creatures") the pilot reached the release, opened `Choose an option for
    Starstorm:` — `1. Cast Card Normally` / `2. cycling` / `3. Decline` — took row 1
    believing it spent the card the same way, and announced X=0: `auto=damage:X
    all(creature)` draws nothing, only `autohand=__CYCLING__({3})` draws, and it had
    four mana for a {3} cycle. It stayed on four lands with two Rorix and two
    Siege-Gang stranded and lost 19 to -23. The guide had a verdict for WHETHER to
    spend the card and none for WHICH ROW spends it. When a card has two or more menu
    paths that dispose of it, the section that governs the card enumerates them by
    their rendered row names and gives each a verdict, including the degenerate one
    (a value of 0, a mode with no legal target). "Do X" is not executable when two
    rows both look like X. Extends #37.

58. A BLOCK SECTION'S FIRST STEP SAYS WHICH BODY IS SPENT, AS AN ORDERED NUMBERED
    STEP BEFORE ANY TRADE EVALUATION. At 12 life against one attacker dealing 3, with
    the header saying "NOT lethal" and fourteen blockers offered — thirteen of them
    free tokens, every row reading `(your blocker dies, attacker lives)` — deck123
    spent Bloodline Keeper (its engine, wearing the Greaves), killed both, and never
    made another token. Its "block with your TOKENS first" instruction was present,
    third in a five-bullet prose list, surrounded by trade language. State the body
    choice as step 1, with the render-readable discriminator (a token row prints no
    mana cost; a card row prints one), and only then rank trades. Priority statements
    buried mid-list lose to the evaluation vocabulary around them. Pairs with #39:
    the card/token distinction governs SELECTION as well as prohibition.

59. WALK A NEW EDIT AGAINST THE RENDER'S OWN VOCABULARY BEFORE SHIPPING IT — FIND THE
    FALSIFIER BY READING, NOT BY WAITING. deck130 shipped two wave-44 edits written
    from one real incident each, and one corpus produced a clean falsification of
    both by CORRECT play: "CHUMP THE BIGGEST ATTACKER" named an attacker tagged
    `[NONE of your available blockers can block this attacker ...]`, so obeying the
    letter loses on the spot (the pilot blocked the only legal attacker and survived
    at 3); "take any block where both die" named Siege-Gang Commander against a Wolf
    token, and the pilot correctly answered `BLOCKS: none` to keep the card whose
    ability needs it alive. Both generalised one word too far — "biggest" without
    "blockable", "creature" without "card or token". Before shipping an edit written
    from one incident, walk the render vocabulary on the same screen for the strings
    that could make the new sentence false: the legality tags (`[NONE of your
    available blockers can block ...]`, the `may block` list), the body-class
    distinction, the keyword list. This is #30's "record a falsifier" turned into an
    authoring step. Its review-side companion (deck126's Chromatic Lantern rule,
    failed 2/14 by two correct casts): before recording a behavioural prediction as
    FAILED, check that the rendered field the rule points at carries the quantity the
    decision turns on — a presence line (`colours you can make: {g}{b}{w}`) does not
    answer a count question ("do I have two black sources"), and a rule keyed to the
    wrong field is violated by correct play while the review entrenches it.

60. STATE A NULL ANSWER'S PRECONDITION BEFORE THE PROCEDURE IT RELEASES, NOT AT THE
    BOTTOM OF IT. deck152 answered `BLOCKS: none` twice in one ten-turn game — once
    past a `(both die)` its rung 2 takes, once at "you would be at 5" against a rung-3
    floor of 9 — and both replies were two lines long with no reference to the ladder
    at all. The permission to answer none is the LAST line of a 25-line ladder; the
    model never got there, and the 3 damage that block erases is exactly the margin
    between -2 and +1. Put the exit condition first, phrased as one comparison against
    a printed number. A procedure whose exit is buried at the bottom is exited before
    it is entered. Cheap review companion: a `BLOCKS:` reply that never mentions the
    header's own "you would be at N" number is a measurable skipped-procedure signal
    (2 for 2 here). Extends #24's "the clause nearest the decision wins" into a
    placement rule.

61. EVERY NUMERIC THRESHOLD SHIPS WITH A ONE-LINE WHY IN THAT WAVE'S edit-texts.md.
    deck123's 12-creature token cap held 42/42 in earlier waves and was violated ten
    times in this one, every violation the better play by odds, in two games it won.
    No wave-40..44 artefact records what the 12 is FOR — it is not prompt size (the
    seat's largest prompt is 19,155 chars and the ranged collapse keeps wide boards
    flat) — so no reviewer could raise it, lower it or cut it on evidence; it could
    only be re-obeyed. An unrecorded threshold is a standing tax on every later
    review. Write it as "T = <number> because <observable that goes wrong above it>",
    so a later wave can re-derive it when the deck's rates change. #34 already
    requires this for rate-crossing thresholds; it generalises to all of them.

62. ONE ORDERED CAST LIST PER GUIDE; CARD SECTIONS HANG OFF ITS NUMBERED ENTRIES.
    deck146's casting advice is correct in five separate places (#1 RULE for removal,
    DEPLOY for cheap bodies, PLANESWALKERS, VENTURE, CLOSE THE GAME) and there is no
    order between them. At 5 mana with Lolth and Kaya both on the menu and a Fate
    Unraveler on their board, it cast a Barrowin whose own option row read `{right
    now: returns NOTHING - your graveyard has no creature cards}`, planned "cast
    Lolth next turn", was at 1 mana two turns later, and died with both walkers in
    hand. Nothing was violated; the model resolved a collision of five imperatives by
    narrative fit (#27). deck162, which carries a single numbered cast order, runs
    17/20 on it in the same corpus and deck146 has no comparable metric because it
    has no comparable rule. Every guide carries exactly one ordered cast list covering
    its main-phase cast asks, and every card-level section is detail hanging off a
    numbered entry, never an independent imperative. This also yields a per-deck
    compliance metric (first-matching-line obedience) that scattered advice cannot.

63. THE DEFINITION OF DONE COUNTS OFFERS, NOT ONLY OBEDIENCE. Two cheap corpus counts
    that catch defects no obedience metric can see. Per card: `Cast Silverquill
    Command` was offered 13 times and taken 0, violating nothing — all three of its
    guide rules are restrictions, so it scores 13/13 while the card never gets cast.
    Report offer/take for every card the guide gives a rule to; rules plus a 0% take
    rate is #36's prohibition-only defect at card scale. Per section: report
    sends-per-attack-window and blocks-per-block-window as raw counts, per deck, every
    wave — deck162's restored affirmative rung shows as 12 sends in 12 windows against
    wave 44's 2 of 6, which is the cheapest available test for a prohibition-only
    combat section and a defect signal before anyone reads a reply.

64. "VIOLATED-UNPUNISHED" IS ITS OWN VERDICT, DISTINCT FROM PASS AND FAIL. deck162
    broke its collapsed-tag gate at a printed `GANG BLOCK: their 2 biggest together
    deal 5, enough to kill this attacker`, the opponent chose a lone block, the
    attacker lived and the deck won; it broke its engine brake three times in the
    exact shape the guide names and won that game too; deck123 broke its 12-creature
    cap ten times across two wins. Reviewers need somewhere to put "the rule was
    broken and nothing happened" so it does not silently accumulate as evidence for
    loosening — #45 forbids closing a lane on a low-power sample and 67 grades by
    odds, but neither gives the cell a name. Record the odds argument in the same cell
    as the outcome. A gate is never relaxed on a favourable violation; it may be
    relaxed on a convergent odds argument, which is a different claim with a different
    denominator.

65. WHEN A SHIPPED PER-DECISION TEACH MOVES ITS COUNT LESS THAN ABOUT A QUARTER OVER A
    FULL WAVE, STOP REWORDING AND ROUTE IT TO THE REPRESENTATION LAYER. Wave 44's Hive
    edit was keyed to a rendered field, stated in two places including the
    quick-reference list, and said exactly the right thing: find the Hive on your
    battlefield line, if it reads (3/3) pass; never animate in upkeep. Result:
    redundant animations 12 -> 10, upkeep animations 19 -> 18, out of 27 taken from 78
    offers, with two Silverquill Commands uncast in hand throughout. The teach is not
    wrong and not unread — it is competing with an option row that reappears every
    priority pass and says nothing about state. The engine's own conventions already
    put state on the row that changes value (`{target text:}`, `{right now: returns
    NOTHING}`, `{X pricing:}`); extend the convention rather than the prose. This is
    #26 one layer down: a fact that must beat an option row has to be ON the option
    row.

66. A MULLIGAN SECTION IS AN ODDS COMPARISON READ OFF THE PREGAME HEADER'S OWN FIELDS,
    NOT A LAND-COUNT BAND — AND NO FLOOR MOVES ON ONE WINDOW, IN EITHER DIRECTION.
    Fair hands are live for a second corpus: 8 mulligans in 42 seats, opener land
    counts 0-6, and the floors were violated in BOTH directions with the odds running
    against the guide text about as often as against the pilot. deck125 shipped a
    3-land seven whose cheapest spell was mana value 4 and whose coverage line read
    "Playing every land in this hand would not cover any spell in it" — a ship the
    odds favour against a floor that keeps 2-5. deck146 shipped a 2-land seven whose
    cheapest spell was mana value 4 — same shape, and its own floor keeps it. deck162
    bottomed a LAND from a 5-land keep against an unqualified "never bottom a land",
    and the deviation was right. The land count alone does not answer the question;
    the engine already prints the three fields that do — `Your hand (7 cards), counted
    by the engine: N lands, M spells`, `Mana sources among those lands, counted by the
    engine: {W} 2, {U} 2`, and `Playing every land in this hand would cover the cost
    of: ...` / `would not cover any spell in it`. Write the keep test as a comparison
    over those fields (what does this hand DO if the missing lands arrive, and how
    many draws does the wait cost) with the land count as the first, cheapest branch.
    #38's FORM survives intact — the floor is still an imperative the executor
    performs and stops on, never a declarative about which hands are keepable — and so
    does its anti-n=1 core: a floor is moved only on convergent evidence (two or more
    windows, or two or more seats), never from a single window and never to match
    observed behaviour. #38's owner-routing half is RETIRED: there is no owner channel
    for deck strategy, and a question parked there is a question nobody answers. The
    reviewer decides from the odds at the window and records the decision with its
    rationale.

67. THE MULLIGAN SECTION OWNS EVERY ASK DOWN TO `bottom`, AND THE CHAIN STOPS AT THE
    SECOND LOOK. Two seats reached FOUR cards this corpus — deck123 (3 mulligans, then
    bottomed Damnation, Vision Skeins and Idyllic Tutor, i.e. both of its ways to find
    a token-maker, keeping three lands and an Intruder Alarm its own guide calls a
    card that does nothing alone; lost 42-0) and deck146 (3 mulligans from a
    `(keeping 5)` window holding two Plains and a castable Nadaar, in flat violation of
    its own STEP 1; lost at -41). Both lost. The London mulligan already lets a 7-card
    look be shaved to 6, so a third look buys a fresh seven at the price of two cards
    that the shave would have cost one: guides state a hard STOP — at `(keeping 5)` or
    lower, keep any hand holding at least one land, and read no further. And the
    section does not end at the keep (#37): it says what happens at the `bottom` ask
    too, in a priority order that names the deck's enablers, with the land carve-out
    deck146 already carries and deck162 lacked ("never bottom a land unless the hand
    you keep would still hold at least four"), and a floor on spells so the pilot
    cannot bottom its way to an uncastable hand. deck162's Rule 3 and its mulligan
    section never met and it bottomed a Shield Sphere it is told to cast on sight;
    that is the same defect one wave on.

=====================================================================
EDITION AMENDMENTS — wave-46 (2026-08-26) — THIRD FAIR-HAND CORPUS
=====================================================================
Corpus `matchups-20260826-155842`, binary master 486c83189 (lanes F/G/H/I + wave-45
lane E), 2113 decisions / 42 seat logs, 6 fallbacks (0.28%), 21 games all natural, 20
mulligan windows. First corpus on the wave-45 reviewer guides AND the reviewer
boundary pass (3ca0b2622). Merge rule unchanged from waves 44-45: an amendment ships
on convergence across two or more seats, or on one decisive falsification (a rule that
cost a game, or a measured N-of-N obedience that ran the wrong way). Ownership note
(owner doctrine, 2026-08-26): the deck REVIEWER owns every guide change, this skill and
the general strategy are synthesis's, and the CORE LOOP — engine mechanics, LLM UX,
bugs — is the purpose the reviews feed. Nothing below routes a deck-content question to
the owner; there is no such channel, and every question is decided from the corpus.

68. A RELEASE CONDITION IS A JOIN BETWEEN THE GUIDE AND THE DECK LIST, AND AN
    UNREACHABLE RELEASE IS AN UNCONDITIONAL RULE WEARING A CONDITION. deck123's
    CHECK 1 held its attack "until a Tragic Slip, a Damnation or an edict has taken the
    LAST of them off that line" over a name list containing Sanguine Bond and Exquisite
    Blood — both `type=Enchantment`, and deck123's sixty contain no enchantment removal.
    The pilot obeyed for eight turns with fourteen Humans on the board, then cast
    Damnation with the plan "to wipe the board, removing the Sanguine Bond", killed its
    own fourteen creatures, and lost 42-0 with both enchantments still on the
    battlefield one window later. The card-fact discipline (#43) verifies the CARD; it
    does not verify that this deck can ACT on it. Before shipping any "until X is
    removed / answered / dealt with" clause, check the sixty for a card that can remove
    a thing of X's TYPE, and when there is none, do not write the sentence as a wait —
    the wait becomes permanent AND it silently teaches that the named removal works on
    the named card, which is the second half of what went wrong here. Same check for
    "hold this until you can pay for it" and "wait for a second copy".

69. THE RULE FOR THE FIRST ASK GOES AT THE TOP OF THE FILE, AND A RULE THAT GOVERNS A
    REPEATED IDENTICAL ASK MUST SURVIVE ITS OWN CARRIED PLAN. The wave-45 boundary pass
    gave deck123 a correct, keyed, imperative mulligan chain stop — as STEP 1 of the
    MULLIGAN section, at line ~340 of a 424-line file. Two of six games then ran the
    chain to ZERO cards (seven mulligans, entire hand bottomed, lost 42-0) and to ONE
    card (six mulligans, one decision made all game, dead turn 13); nine looks at
    `(keeping 5)` or lower were answered Mulligan with a land in hand, three of them
    holding three lands and a coverage line naming castable spells. The text was right
    and nothing about its wording would have improved with another pass. Two placement
    facts caused it. (a) For an ask that fires BEFORE turn one, "put the rule where its
    trigger is" (#60) means before the deck thesis and everything downstream of it — the
    reader has no board yet and no reason to have read a section named for a phase of
    the game. (b) The pre-game chain is the one place in the loop where an IDENTICAL ask
    repeats with the pilot's own carried plan re-shown as an answer to it: deck123 wrote
    "Mulligan to find a hand with 4+ lands" at look 2 and re-emitted that exact sentence
    as its reply at looks 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7. A rule for such an ask is written to be read
    against a carried plan that argues the other way — name the trap ("a plan you wrote
    about a hand you have already shipped is not about this hand") and make the stop an
    imperative about what to ANSWER, not a fact about which hands are keepable (#38).
    The render half is docketed; the placement half is the guide's and is cheap.

70. AN EXCEPTION LIVES ABOVE THE IMPERATIVE IT EXCEPTS, AND AN UNCONDITIONAL RUNG
    DELETES EVERY CONDITIONED RUNG BENEATH IT. Three seats, one shape. deck126's RULE #5
    opens `Assign EVERY blocker the list offers you, in every combat:` and puts the
    survival carve-out thirty lines below under a heading of its own; both blocks in the
    game it lost obeyed the imperative and violated the carve-out (a 0/4 wall traded for
    ONE point of stopped damage against a 1/1 first-strike deathtoucher; a 0/3 wall took
    the 3-damage attacker that kills it over the 1-damage attacker it survives; the
    board was empty two turns later and the seat was dead on turn 10). deck162's ladder
    opens "1. A line ending '(you kill it, your blocker lives)' — take that block. Free
    kill, every time", so rung 3's life-8 clause was unreachable on the screen where it
    mattered: it took a free kill on a 2/2 while 6 damage walked past, 12 -> 4, dead two
    turns later. Both rungs are individually correct; the LADDER is what is wrong. Rule:
    before shipping an unconditional early rung or a blanket opening imperative, ask
    which later clause it pre-empts; every survival condition, carve-out or exception
    that can fire on the same screen becomes its own numbered step ABOVE it, reusing the
    number the lower rung already carries so the guide ships one threshold, not two, and
    the imperative is then worded as conditional on the step above it. The deck126
    control in the same corpus shows exactly when the ordering matters: the same
    carve-out FIRED correctly on a Vampire B-line and LOST on a wall B-line, and the
    only difference is that the wall's row carries a rival printed quantity
    (`[deals 0 - ... but it STOPS all N damage from reaching you]`). An exception loses
    to a blanket imperative precisely when the render supplies a rival number, which is
    the case in which the guide must state precedence outright, in the render's own
    vocabulary.

71. AN ABSOLUTE THAT CAN FORBID A WIN NEEDS ITS LETHAL CARVE-OUT AS A NUMBERED CHECK
    ABOVE IT, NOT A CLAUSE INSIDE IT. deck146's Hive CHECK 1 ("If it says Upkeep, the
    answer is PASS ... There is no exception to this") is a GOOD rule — it took wasted
    manland activations from 27-of-78 to 1-of-46 in one wave. It also declined the game:
    `priority` seq 50 and 51, turn 23, opponent at 1 life, the Hive untapped with four
    sources up, animating is exactly lethal, and both answers were `pass`; the opponent
    went 1 -> 6 -> 11 -> 17 -> 25 and won on turn 41. #30 requires a recorded falsifier
    for every absolute; this names the one falsifier that recurs and makes it an
    authoring step. For each absolute you write, ask: can a board exist on which obeying
    this declines a win THIS TURN? If yes, the lethal check is a numbered check above the
    absolute — a reader who stops at the first matching check must reach it first — and
    it reuses the guide's existing lethal wording, so the deck ships one lethal test.
    Companion falsifier to watch for: a carve-out over-firing on boards that are not
    lethal.

72. EVERY RULE INPUT IS A NUMBER OR A TAG THE PROMPT PRINTS — NO DERIVED COUNTS, NO
    RUNNING TALLIES, NO MOOD WORDS. Three seats measured the same law from three
    directions in one corpus.
    (a) DERIVED COUNTS. deck125's rules keyed to a printed field went to ceiling — land
    drop 40/40, sweeper 0-creature gate 123/123, the counter `[defender]` clause 39/39,
    Staff ping 75/75 — while its X-sizing rule, whose input is "count the cards on
    `Your hand:`", conformed 4/17. The direct proof that this is perception and not
    disobedience: 3 of the 4 replies that stated a hand size in words stated it WRONG,
    once as "hand size 6" against an eleven-card list.
    (b) RUNNING TALLIES. deck152's "from the fifth counter on, put it on a SECOND
    creature" requires remembering placements across turns; seven consecutive counters
    went onto Sigarda (4/4 -> 11/11) in one game. There is no memory between asks. The
    option row prints each creature's CURRENT size on every one of those windows.
    (c) MOOD WORDS. deck146's "take it most turns you are not desperate for that life"
    produced Lolth-0 activations at 16, 12, 9, 5 and 2 life and the seat died at 0.
    "Desperate", "when you can afford it", "spend it freely early" are not on the screen;
    a printed life total is.
    Rule: when a rule's input is not rendered, the guide's job is to SAY so and pick a
    constant or re-key to a rendered proxy — never to instruct the pilot to count harder
    — and to record a SUNSET TEST naming the render that would retire the constant. The
    missing render goes to the ledger as its own item; it never enters the guide as an
    instruction. #33 made this ruling for reserved mana and #65 for a teach that will not
    move; this is the general form, and it is the highest-yield single check in the
    Definition of Done.

73. WHERE A RULE BRANCHES TO SEVERAL THRESHOLDS OFF ONE RENDERED FIELD, THE BRANCH IS
    THE FAILURE — COLLAPSE IT TO ONE CONSTANT. deck125's Staff of Nin tap-out rule ("8
    with an Essence Scatter, 9 with a Cancel or Dream Fracture, 11 with only a Fall of
    the Gavel, 6 with none") has read 6/11 -> 3-4/7 -> 4/7 across three waves while every
    single-field rule on the same seat reached ceiling. The four conforming casts were at
    `Mana available:` 17, 10, 13 and 22; the three violations at 6, 7 and 6. A flat 9
    separates them perfectly and costs one turn on an Essence-Scatter-only hand.
    #48 collapsed the ARITHMETIC to one operation; this collapses the CASE ANALYSIS to
    one number. The count of numbers in a rule is itself a variable, and the strictest
    constant that reproduces the corpus's correct verdicts beats a correct branch. Keep
    the reason for the constant in one clause after the rule (#48), and record it as a
    threshold WHY (#61).

74. A RULE THAT NAMES A CLASS MUST NAME MEMBERS OF IT. deck125's counter section holds
    two let-it-resolve clauses eight lines apart, read by the same model in the same
    windows. The `[defender]` clause names Pride Guardian, Wall of Omens, Fog Bank and
    Shield Sphere by name with their P/T, and went from 4/33 violations to 0/39. The
    `anything printed (artifact) with no P/T` clause names nothing, and leaked 2 of 39
    counters onto mana artifacts (Chromatic Lantern, Talisman of Impulse), one of them
    inside a loss. An abstract class does not fire; the same class with two named cards
    and one sentence of consequence does. This is #49's tag rule from the other side:
    when there IS no tag, names are the substitute — never an unexampled category.

75. A BY-NAME PROPERTY LIST IS A STATIC CLAIM IN A GAME WHERE PERMANENTS REWRITE EACH
    OTHER'S PROPERTIES; VERIFY IT AGAINST THE RENDER, NOT ONLY AGAINST THE PRIMITIVE
    THAT WROTE IT. deck126's Lantern gate read "the lands of yours that make black are
    Bayou, Scrubland, Woodland Cemetery, Isolated Chapel, the Swamp and Urborg. SAVANNAH
    AND SUNPETAL GROVE DO NOT". Every fact is right about each card in isolation, and the
    list is FALSE on a board holding Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth (`auto=lord(land)
    transforms((swamp))` — every land is a Swamp, so Savannah and Sunpetal Grove do make
    {B}). Both of the guide's worst Lantern casts happened on an Urborg board; the
    render's per-colour clause read `{B} 3` and `{B} 6` and was right in both windows
    while the guide's by-name "2" was wrong, and the gate failed 5/5. #43 required every
    colour claim to be written from the primitives; this adds the second half: where the
    engine renders a COUNT of the property, key the rule to the count and DELETE the
    enumeration; where it does not, write the enumeration with its modifier class named
    ("...unless a permanent is changing land types"). A by-name list that a lord or
    transform effect can falsify is a rule that will be wrong exactly on the boards where
    it is applied hardest.

76. AN ORDERED FIRST-MATCH LIST IS A TOTAL FUNCTION OR IT IS NOT A LIST. #62 required
    exactly one ordered cast list per guide; deck146 shipped one and it holds 46 of 73
    own-turn cast asks — but NINE of the 27 breaks are cards the list does not contain
    (`Cast Silverquill Silencer` taken 8 times, `Cast Emeria's Call` once), and most of
    those casts were good plays. When the executor must go outside a list that told it
    "stop there — do not read the rest", the instruction it abandons is the first-match
    discipline itself, not that one entry. Before shipping a first-match list, enumerate
    every card in the sixty that can appear as a `Cast ...` option and confirm each is
    matched by some entry; a card with no entry is a defect in the LIST. Close the set
    with a named catch-all and make "cast nothing" the LAST entry rather than a
    tiebreaker available at any depth. Related same-seat break: 10 of the other 27 are
    declines of a card the list DOES rank, whose rule is an imperative with no
    observable — such an entry is re-keyed to the option list itself ("if it is printed
    and nothing above it matched, take it"), per 72.

77. REFUTE THE PRINCIPLE, NOT THE INSTANCE — THE NEXT CORPUS WILL PRODUCE A FRESH
    INSTANCE. deck146's STOP already refuses "outnumbering them protects my card"; the
    wave-46 break used the identical falsehood in a new shape: *"Attack with Nadaar,
    Goblin, and Triumphant Adventurer. Triumphant Adventurer blocks Fate Unraveler
    (trades)"* — a different ATTACKER of its own would absorb the blocker. An attacking
    creature does not block, and THEY choose which attacker to stop. Both sentences
    reduce to one error (assuming control over the defender's allocation, #54) and the
    guide had refuted only one instance of it. When you write a refutation, state the
    PRINCIPLE the false sentence violates and then list the instances seen so far.
    "THEY choose which attacker their blocker stops" generalises; "sending three when
    they have one blocker does not protect mine" does not. #28 says quote the shape of
    the reasoning and forbid it by name; this says the NAME must be the principle.
    Watch item, one window, not yet an amendment: a ban that keeps being reasoned around
    may be sitting on a false RULES belief — deck146's Vanishing Verse ban went 22/23 and
    the one break says out loud *"Exile Nadaar ... to cycle it back to hand"*. Writing
    the belief and refuting it ("exile is not a bounce — the card is gone") is cheaper
    than adding force to the ban. Re-check in wave 47.

78. A POSTURE RULE SELECTS AMONG THE OPTIONS THE PRICE RULES ALLOW; IT NEVER ADDS
    OPTIONS THE PRICES REFUSE. deck152 carries a lifegain-wall PRICE rule ("at two or
    more, the attack PAYS them") and a matchup POSTURE rule ("vs A LIFE-TO-DAMAGE
    CONVERTER ... the correct posture is the most aggressive one available: attack with
    everything that is not held home by a stop"). Both fired on the same screen for three
    consecutive combats; the posture won; the seat spent FIFTEEN life on its own attacks
    (20 -> 11 -> 5) while the opponent gained the same amount, and lost at -1 from a board
    it was ahead on. deck162 lost the mirror in one turn (19 -> 0) having neither rule.
    A mood beats a price in prose every time, because the mood sentence is shorter and
    reads like a conclusion. Rule: when you add a posture or matchup rule, name the price
    rules in the same guide it will be read against and state the direction of the
    interaction. And where the interaction is genuinely multiplicative — a converter of
    THEIRS doubling every life they gain — say the arithmetic, because that is the case
    where the price rule must get STRICTER under the aggressive posture, which is the
    opposite of what the mood word suggests.

79. THE GOVERNING NUMBER IS WRITTEN FIRST, AS AN INSTRUCTION ABOUT WHAT TO EMIT.
    deck152's block ladder carries both the floor ("take this block when N is 9 or less")
    and an explicit arithmetic step ("read the header's 'you would be at N', compare N to
    9, and answer") — and both sit BELOW a 25-line ladder. Second corpus running, the seat
    answered a bare `BLOCKS: none` at a header reading "you would be at 8 — NOT lethal",
    with the reply *"I will take the 6 damage, dropping to 8 life."* It printed the number
    and never compared it, and that was the margin it died by. #60 said put the exit
    condition first; this sharpens it into a form the reviewer can grep: where a decision
    has one governing number, the section OPENS with "the first line of your answer is
    <the number>". A number the executor did not WRITE is a number it did not use, and
    the absence of that number in a reply becomes a falsifiable defect a later wave can
    count without reading a word of reasoning.

80. EVERY HARD FLOOR NAMES ITS REGIME. "NEVER bottom a land unless the hand you keep
    would still hold at least FOUR" is correct at six and five cards and absurd at four —
    where deck152 correctly bottomed three lands from a five-land keep, and obeying would
    have left it a four-card hand of four lands. The regime is on the screen: the ask
    prints "You will be left with an N-card hand". State the regime in the same sentence
    as the floor and key it to something the prompt prints. A floor whose regime is
    unstated cannot be falsified — every violation reads as either "the rule is wrong" or
    "the pilot is wrong", and the corpus cannot tell a reviewer which, which is exactly
    the ambiguity #66 forbids resolving by moving the number.

81. RUN A COVERAGE DIFF AGAINST THE OTHER GUIDES IN THE POOL BEFORE TUNING ANYTHING A
    GUIDE ALREADY HAS. deck162 went 5-1 to 3-3 while every wave-45 edit it received held
    or improved (Rule 1 punisher-first 17/20 -> 20/21; the LETHAL survival gate PASS on
    its first live window). All three losses trace to sections the guide has never
    contained, and a sibling guide in the same pool has each one: no land rule (35/39
    drops, three declines in the game it lost; deck146, which has one, is 43/43), no
    lifegain/converter price (19 -> 0 in a single combat with the converter line printed),
    and a keep-it-home rule that names one card instead of the role (swung its only
    untapped body at 3 life, dead at -2). The wave-45 pass concluded "nothing to add"
    because everything the guide HAD was in good shape — a different question from what
    it lacks. Before revising, list the decision surfaces the engine can present (land
    drop, mana line, cast order, attack tags, blocking ladder, mulligan, bottoming, each
    named opposing mechanic) and mark which pool guides have a rule for each. A blank
    cell is a finding, and it outranks tuning a cell that is already full. #52 made a
    newly rendered STRING obligate every guide that can see it; this generalises the
    register to every decision surface, and it makes "a guide that scores well on every
    rule it has" a testable claim rather than a compliment.

82. A RULE KEYED TO A RENDERED TOKEN MUST BRANCH ON THAT TOKEN'S ABSENCE. Every rung of
    deck162's ATTACKING section keys off what the `their untapped blockers` tag SAYS.
    Twice in one game the A-line carried NO tag at all (the opponent's battlefield line
    read `(0 permanents listed)`), which is free damage by construction — no rung matched,
    and the decision fell to a mood ("preserve Fate Unraveler as a blocker") against a
    player with no creatures; attack rate fell 12/12 -> 6/8 and both declines are this
    shape. deck126 threw away a free lifelink point the same way at an untagged A-line.
    The executor does not read "the tag is missing" as "there is nothing to fear"; an
    unmatched decision is decided by narrative fit (#27). Write the ABSENT case
    explicitly for every rendered token a rule reads. This is the mirror of the trust
    doctrine: the surface owes the model truth, and the guide owes the model a branch for
    every state that surface can be in, including not being there. (The render-side
    complement — printing the affirmative form instead of nothing — is on the docket; the
    guide branch is owed either way, because absence is also what a future render change
    can produce.)

83. A ROLE RULE IS DEFINED BY A COUNT, NOT BY A CARD NAME. deck162's "At 2 life your Fate
    Unraveler is also your blocker" is exactly right about the ROLE and names one card.
    The card that lost the game in that role was Master of the Feast — which the same
    guide separately calls "your fastest clock ... swing with it every single turn". A
    card-named rule has a coverage hole the moment the board changes, and the executor
    reads the other card's own enthusiastic line instead. Define the role off something
    the prompt prints ("count the untapped, non-summoning-sick creatures on YOUR
    battlefield line; if that count is one"), then name cards as examples. Same law as
    72(c), applied to WHICH BODY rather than to a quantity, and it pairs with #39's card/
    token distinction: role, class and body-kind are all read off the render or not at all.

84. A THRESHOLD'S SUNSET IS TWO-SIDED, AND ITS WHY IS RE-MEASURED WHETHER IT CONFIRMS OR
    REFUTES. Wave 45 raised deck123's token cap 12 -> 20 with the WHY "the ranged-collapse
    render holds a 22-permanent board to ~19k chars, so board width is not costing
    decision quality below that" and a sunset reading "if wave 46 shows 0 violations at
    20, wave 47 deletes it". Wave 46 produced SIX crossings at 20-23 (both games won) AND
    SIX declines at counts of 3 to 15 where the rule says take the line. The literal
    sunset (0 violations) was not met, so a mechanical reading KEEPS the number — and the
    second signal is the stronger evidence that the number is inert: it is not being used
    as a rule in either direction, and it was being credited for a stop the pilot makes
    for its own reasons. Count crossings ABOVE a threshold and compliance failures BELOW
    it; a threshold crossed unpunished and disobeyed underneath is inert regardless of the
    crossing count, and is REPLACED by a condition with evidence (deck123 replaced the
    headcount with power-vs-their-printed-life), which satisfies #35's do-not-delete-the-
    only-stop. Second half, from the same evidence: the WHY's observable is re-measured
    the next wave and the number recorded. Wave 46 measured this one and it was TRUE (the
    largest deck123 prompt at 23+ creatures is 19,082 chars, identical to its largest at
    12+), and CONFIRMING it is what removed the last argument for keeping any headcount.
    A confirmed WHY that no longer implies its rule is a deletion, not a renewal.

85. THE SECOND IDENTICAL FAILURE ENDS THE GUIDE LANE: WRITE THE RE-FORM, AND RECORD IN
    THE SAME EDIT WHAT WOULD SHOW THE LANE IS EXHAUSTED AND WHICH RENDER ITEM IS THE
    REMEDY. deck130's Starstorm cycling rung failed identically in wave 45 and wave 46 —
    cast row, `Choose an option for Starstorm:`, "Cast Card Normally", announce, X=0. Between
    the corpora the guide gained `CASTING IT AT X=0 IS NOT CYCLING`, a description of the
    menu by name, and `NEVER announce X=0`; in wave 46 the pilot's own plan read "to cycle
    it ... per Strategy Guide Rule #1" and it took the wrong row anyway. The menu's two
    rows are bare (`1. Cast Card Normally` / `2. cycling`) in a loop where the row before
    and the row after both carry full annotations. #65 routes a teach that moves less than
    about a quarter to the representation layer; this is the zero-movement, twice-identical
    form, and it makes the hand-off explicit so wave N+1 does not spend its edit budget on
    a fourth restatement. A guide can change what the pilot DECIDES; it cannot change what
    the pilot can SEE on the row.

86. WHEN A RUNG FAILS, CHECK WHETHER THE GUIDE SENTENCE AND THE RENDER'S OWN LEADING
    CLAUSE PUSH THE SAME WAY. deck130's X-pricing cast row leads with `smallest X that
    kills an OPPONENT creature: X=1`; its guide said "pick the smallest X that reaches the
    toughness you must kill". Both are true and neither is wrong alone; together they made
    "smallest" the whole decision. The pilot announced X=1 where X=2 killed the token-maker
    as well for `YOURS: none` at zero cost (it controlled no creatures), the Doomsayer lived,
    made twenty-one more tokens behind an Intruder Alarm, and the game ended 19 to -31.
    #23 established that a guide must not push the same way as a menu's own headline; this
    makes it a diagnostic step at every rung failure, and adds the routing half: a guide
    qualifying its own prompt is a weaker fix than a prompt that states both facts in the
    same clause shape, so the render item is FILED as well as the edit written.

87. AN ENGINE-SIDE SUPPRESSION CHANGES A RULE'S DENOMINATOR, NOT ITS RATE — REPORT BOTH
    POPULATIONS OR REPORT NEITHER. deck126's `Add N green mana with Overgrown Battlement`
    discipline reads 1/16 this wave against 2/39 last wave, and the two fractions are over
    different populations: the wave-46 mana-only auto-pass removed 180 windows before they
    reached the model (all 180 at this one seat, ~85% of its priority churn). Neither
    number is a trend and neither reviewer should report one. The same trap caught an
    engine prediction in the same corpus — "take-rate on surviving windows unchanged" was
    scored FAIL against a raw priority take-rate that rose 47.8% -> 62.3%, which is the
    denominator effect the gate was built to produce. Whenever a lane suppresses,
    collapses or filters a window class, every rate that class touches is restated on a
    like-for-like basis before it is compared, and a wave that cannot do so reports counts
    only. Small guide-side corollary the evidence supports: once the engine suppresses a
    window class, SEEING one of those windows is itself information ("something else was
    on the menu too"), and a guide may say so.

88. A STOP CONDITION IS TESTABLE ONLY AGAINST A NUMBER THE ACTION ITSELF MOVES.
    deck123's RULE 1 stopped the token engine on "the printed power of the creatures that
    do NOT read summoning sick, versus the opponent's life". Every token the loop makes IS
    summoning sick, so taking the line does not change the quantity in the test: P was
    constant across 1,868 activations of one row in one turn, the pilot's own plan said it
    would stop and attack, and the game DEAD-LOOPED (no gameend, invariant 00 failed,
    ~9 h wall, 48 M prompt characters). The opponent's-turn branch was worse: it read "take
    it anyway ... it costs nothing", which is unbounded by construction. So, before shipping
    any rule of the form "keep doing X until N": check that TAKING X CHANGES N. A stop
    written on a quantity the action leaves untouched is not a weak stop, it is not a stop
    at all — the pilot can obey it forever and be inside a loop while doing so. Prefer the
    number the action increments and the prompt prints (a header count, a `[repeat: N times
    already]` tag) over the number that is strategically nicer but static (power that
    excludes what you just made, mana you did not spend, damage you have not dealt). If the
    meaningful number really is the right one, pair it with a MONOTONE tripwire on the
    mechanical one. The same defect in miniature is wave 46's mulligan chain — "keep until
    the hand is keepable" at least tested a property mulliganing changes, which is why it
    ran to seven and not to 1,868. Scope note from the same corpus (see #90): a tripwire
    keyed to a per-ability counter is only monotone for THAT ability; where two abilities
    feed one loop the tag under-counts, and the board-side count is the reliable half.

89. WHEN A RULE NEEDS A QUANTITY, TAKE IT FROM THE SURFACE NEAREST THE CHOICE — THE OPTION
    ROW FIRST. deck125's tap-out gate failed FOUR consecutive waves (6/11, 3-4/7, 4/7, 6/7)
    across three formulations: a four-way branch on which counter was held, then a single
    constant (9), then the constant restated in DECIDING SITUATIONS. Every version asked the
    pilot to compare a number it would hold AFTER the cast against a line printed BEFORE it.
    Collapsing to a constant was the right KIND of fix by #62/#73 and it still failed, which
    isolates the variable: the problem was never the size of the computation, it was that
    the answer lived on a different surface from the decision. In the same corpus three rules
    keyed to a field printed ON THE ROW went to ceiling with no guide change at all — X
    sizing 4/17 -> 12/12 once `{X pricing:}` appeared on the row, the land drop 93/93 once
    the ask carried its own consequence sentence, mana-artifact counters 0/28. Preference
    order for a rule input: (a) a number on the OPTION ROW the pilot is about to select;
    (b) a number on a header line in the same prompt; (c) a constant; (d) an arithmetic
    instruction. Moving a failing rule from (c)/(d) to (a) is a DISTINCT and cheaper repair
    than restating it or hoisting it, and it is tried before either. Corollary, and it is a
    standing sweep: when the engine ships a new per-row or per-header field, walk every rule
    that was deriving that quantity — the derivation has become a liability, not redundancy.

90. A RULE KEYED TO A RENDERED STRING QUOTES THE STRING THE EMITTER ACTUALLY PRINTS, AND THE
    QUOTE IS CHECKED AGAINST THE CORPUS BEFORE IT SHIPS. deck146's lifegain-wall rule told
    the pilot to look for a `(blocking trigger:` clause. Lane K's converter fold had changed
    the string on exactly those rows to `(lifelink: they gain N, and their converter takes N
    off you)`. The rule was therefore looking for a substring that was not on the screen, it
    did not fire, the seat sent five attackers, paid ELEVEN life in one swing from 18, and
    lost the game. Both strings were true; only one was printed there. The check is
    mechanical and costs one grep: every literal the guide quotes is counted in the corpus,
    and a literal with zero hits on the rows the rule governs is a defect, not a typo.
    Where a family of strings can appear, the rule names the family ("a `(blocking trigger:`
    clause OR a `(lifelink: they gain` clause"), never one member of it. Sibling evidence,
    recorded not condemned: deck162's mulligan stop keys on `"having already taken 1
    mulligan"` rather than the price row — a different real string with correct content, so
    it is an alternate key, not a break.

91. A RULE MAY NOT BE KEYED TO A COUNT OF ITEMS THE RENDER IS ALLOWED TO COLLAPSE. The same
    deck146 loss carried a second, independent defect: the rule's threshold was "if TWO OR
    MORE blockers on this creature's tag print a `(blocking trigger:` clause". A collapsed
    blocker tag prints EXACTLY ONE blocker (`they have 5 untapped creatures that could block
    this one, biggest Vampire (1/1)`), so the threshold was unsatisfiable BY CONSTRUCTION on
    precisely the wide boards the rule was written for. Before writing "two or more X on the
    tag", check whether that list has a collapsed form. If it does, key the rule to the
    PRESENCE of one X plus the collapse's own count word ("they have N untapped creatures"),
    never to the number of X you can see. Under a collapse, a count you can read is a LOWER
    BOUND; a rule that treats it as the truth is a rule that silently switches off on big
    boards, and the corpus will show it passing its own metric while losing games.
    Sweep form: any pool rule phrased "two or more ... print" over a collapsible list is a
    defect and the sweep should return zero.

92. A TOTAL ORDERED FIRST-MATCH LIST BECOMES THE GUIDE'S ONLY EXECUTABLE ORDERING: EVERY
    CONDITIONAL STATED ELSEWHERE NEEDS A RANK IN IT. deck126's RULE #4 named "the opponent
    controls exactly ONE creature" as a Tribute to Hunger cast condition. It was correct,
    legible, and had NO position in RULE #7, the numbered first-match list the pilot actually
    executes — where Tribute sat at entry 8, below both enchantments, the tutor, four walls,
    Staff, Sorin and the Lantern. Result: **0 of 5** windows where the condition held, one of
    them inside the loss, with the deck's only removal spell in the menu each time. This is a
    COST OF #62/#76's own recommendation and does not repeal them: making the list total is
    right — the same edit took unpaid `Cast nothing` from 24/24 to 4/47 at that seat — but a
    total list becomes the only ordering, and any conditional stated outside it is dead text
    unless it has a rank. Audit form: walk every "cast X when Y" sentence anywhere in the
    guide and name the entry number it lands at. A condition with no landing place is a
    defect, not a redundancy. Whenever #76's roll-call is added, this audit is run in the
    SAME wave.

93. AN EMITTED TOKEN BELONGS TO A RULE, NEVER TO A PREDICTION'S SCORE. Two seats hit this
    from opposite sides in one corpus. deck152's wave-46 prediction had a behavioural half
    (`BLOCKS: none` at a header of 9 or less: 0) that PASSED 0/4, and a vocabulary half
    (every blocks reply names N) that read 0/4 — not one reply quoted the number, and all
    four assignments were correct. A reviewer scoring only the vocabulary half would have
    recorded a total failure of a rule working perfectly: the model routinely acts on a
    surface it never quotes. deck146 shows the other side: its CHECK 0 exception was a
    permission with no observable at all, and within one corpus it became the default answer
    (10 non-lethal Upkeep animations of 12 takes, 40 mana). The resolution is not "demand
    tokens" or "never demand tokens", it is a separation: where a written token is genuinely
    wanted, make EMITTING IT PART OF THE RULE ("write both numbers into your reply; if the
    numbers are not there, the exception did not fire") — an instruction the pilot is told to
    obey. Never make it part of a PREDICTION about a rule that is about something else.
    Score the CHOICE. Where a rule does demand a token, report two numbers next wave, kept
    separate: did the token appear, and did the choice improve.

94. A FRESH-COMPUTED STOP MUST OUTRANK THE CARRIED PLAN, IN ONE SENTENCE, AT THE STOP.
    Removing the carried plan from PREGAME asks produced the cleanest pregame result the
    project has had (8 mulligans corpus-wide, every one a single look, zero chains, against
    wave 46's 9 third-look chains). The same mechanism is alive one layer down and cost
    three separate decisions this corpus: `152 vs146` seq 18 answered `YOUR PLAN ... Attack
    with Hydra and Katilda` verbatim into two A-lines that read `your attacker dies, their
    blocker lives`; `deck130 vs126` seq 37 answered `Cast Starstorm at X=3` verbatim into an
    X=4 row printing a strictly larger free kill list; deck123's edict plans named a body an
    edict cannot choose. In every case the plan was written BEFORE the surface that refutes
    it existed. A general "trust the render" preamble does not carry this — the plan is the
    model's own prior reasoning handed back as context, and it competes with the render on
    equal footing unless a rule says it does not. So: wherever a guide states a per-window
    STOP the engine computes fresh (attacker tags, blocker rows, target legality, X kill
    lists), one sentence AT THE STOP says the plan does not license past it, naming the
    rendered string. The render half is filed as well (#86's routing half) — the two shipped
    fixes of this shape were both render-side.

95. WHEN A RULE ELEVATES A SET, WRITE THE TIEBREAK FOR TWO MEMBERS ON ONE MENU — COMPLIANCE
    COUNTS ARE BLIND TO IT. deck162's RULE 1 ("your three punishers ... if ANY of the three
    is in the list, CAST IT THIS ASK ... ahead of every other card in your deck, at every
    life total, on every board") is the pool's strongest rule and its seat went 4-1. Its ONLY
    loss was scored INSIDE the rule: the menu held two of the three punishers and nothing
    else, so the rule was satisfied by either answer, and the seat took the one with no body
    at 16 life against three unrestricted attackers with zero creatures of its own. It never
    produced a `blockers` record and died at turn 12. A rule with an exhaustive "always" over
    interchangeable members is silent exactly when the set collides with itself, and that
    silence is INVISIBLE in the compliance metric — the rule scores 100% on the window that
    lost the game. So: audit every "always / any of these" rule for the two-members-offered
    case before shipping it, and rank the members by a property the prompt already PRINTS
    (here: the two battlefield lines' own `of which N are creatures` counts), never by
    strength in the abstract. Then check that the tiebreak reaches the executable surface —
    a tiebreak living only in prose while the ordered list keeps the set as one undivided
    entry is #92's defect wearing #95's clothes.

96. ONE SOURCE OF TRUTH PER PROCEDURE: THE CARD SECTION POINTS, IT NEVER RESTATES. deck130's
    rule #2 STEP 1 says "find the row with the LARGEST `kills THEIRS` list whose `YOURS:`
    reads `none`". Its KEY CARDS entry for the same card, 100 lines lower, said "pick the
    smallest X that reaches the toughness you must kill". The pilot answered X=3 with an X=4
    row one line above it reading `kills THEIRS: Pride Guardian x2, Perimeter Captain;
    YOURS: none`. It followed the CARD section — and this is the SECOND consecutive corpus
    in which a deck130 failure traced to a card-section sentence contradicting a rule-section
    procedure (wave 46: Dwarven Blastminer, gated in one place and ungated in his card
    entry, 2/2 violations, one lethal). These guides carry a rules section and a card
    section, and the card section is read at the moment of decision because the card's NAME
    is on the row; any procedure appearing in both is a fork, and the corpus says the card
    entry wins. So a card's entry may NAME the rule that owns a decision ("the X is chosen by
    rule #2 STEP 1") and may never restate the procedure or paraphrase it. Shipping gate:
    for every card named in both a rules section and a card section, diff its two
    appearances; the card section must contain no imperative about WHICH option to pick.
    Two waves running, the highest-yield edit at this seat has been DELETING a card-section
    sentence, not adding one.

97. TWO ABSOLUTES WHOSE CONDITIONS CAN CO-OCCUR NEED THEIR PRECEDENCE WRITTEN AT THE
    COLLISION; A HOIST IS THE WRONG REPAIR FOR A RULE LOSING A CONFLICT. deck125 hoisted its
    Emrakul rule into DECIDING SITUATIONS in wave 46, stated absolutely ("TAKE IT"), and it
    was declined 3 of 4 times in wave 47. Sixteen lines below it, in the SAME section, the
    tap-out gate says absolutely not to cast anything leaving fewer than five untapped
    sources — and a fifteen-mana spell can never leave five. The rules were not ambiguous;
    they were CONTRADICTORY, and the collision was unreachable for the pilot to resolve
    because neither named the other. Before adding or hoisting any absolute ("always",
    "every time", "whatever the numbers say"), scan the same guide for other absolutes whose
    conditions can co-occur, and write the precedence at the point of collision
    ("it also outranks the tap-out gate, and it is the only card in this deck that does").
    The symptom that distinguishes a rule LOSING A CONFLICT from a rule GOING UNREAD is a
    reply that shows no reasoning at all — all three Emrakul declines were bare. Hoisting a
    rule that is losing a conflict just puts it closer to the rule beating it.

98. A RULE STATED ONLY AS ITS EXCEPTION FIRES ONLY AS ITS EXCEPTION — BOTH POLARITIES GO IN
    THE DECIDING SECTION. deck125's Path to Exile section states the power rule and then
    spends four times as many words on the floor that SUPPRESSES it, and DECIDING SITUATIONS
    carried only the suppressing line. Path was taken in 1 of 13 windows at 12 life or less
    with a legal high-power target; the other twelve are one lost game, at 12, 10, 5 and 1
    life, holding three copies. Lightmine Field is the exact mirror at the same seat with the
    same outcome: DECIDING SITUATIONS carried only the POSITIVE line and no stop, and it was
    cast 3/3 into boards it could not touch. So: any rule appearing in the nearest-the-
    decision section appears there with BOTH branches — the condition under which you take
    the action and the condition under which you do not. A single-polarity entry is not a
    compressed rule, it is a DIFFERENT rule. Audit form: grep the deciding section for each
    named card and check that both branches are present. This is #70's ordering rule extended
    to coverage: an exception above its imperative is right, an exception INSTEAD OF its
    imperative is a new failure.

99. A GUIDE STATES WHAT THE RENDER PRINTS AND NEVER WHAT IT DOES NOT. deck125's X section
    asserted in bold that the ask "does NOT print a count of your own hand — so a rule keyed
    to your hand size has no field to stand on". That was TRUE when written and became false
    on 413 of 413 prompts the moment `Your hand (N cards):` shipped. A negative-existence
    claim about the render is more corrosive than a merely stale rule: the trust doctrine
    forbids teaching doubt of a rendered value, and a sentence asserting the render's ABSENCE
    licenses exactly that as soon as the field lands. Where an absence genuinely has to be
    handled, phrase the rule around what IS printed instead (deck125's stack-line rule is the
    right shape's wrong half: recognise a wall by the `{target text:}` it DOES carry, and say
    only that). Standing audit: every wave in which the render changes, sweep all seven
    guides for negative-existence claims (`does not print`, `there is no`, `no field`,
    `the ask omits`) and re-point each one at a printed token or delete it. Every such claim
    that survives is a dated bet against a lane that is actively shipping.

100. RENDERING A FACT DOES NOT STOP THE MODEL RESTATING IT. Lane M shipped own-side
    `{effect:}` text so the pilot could read its own combo off the battlefield line instead
    of re-deriving it in PLAN. The render works — 0 unexplained bare own permanents in 612
    decisions. The behaviour did not move: replies restating the combo's mechanics went
    31/211 (15%) to 34/199 (17%), and p90 reply length was flat (602 -> 615 chars). So a
    render change justified by "the pilot will stop re-deriving X" carries a MEASURED
    re-derivation rate as its falsifier and is not counted as delivered on the strength of
    the string appearing. Reading and restating are different behaviours and the corpus
    separates them cheaply (one regex over replies). Where the actual goal is a shorter
    reply, the lever is in the ASK's instructions, not in the state block. This is #63's
    "count offers, not only obedience" pointed at the render layer, and it is the guide
    lane's own protection: a render item credited on its string leaves a guide rule blamed
    for a behaviour nothing has yet moved.

101. A DISTRIBUTION HEURISTIC WRITTEN FOR THE DEFAULT CASE MUST NAME THE MARKED CASES IT DOES
    NOT COVER. Both of deck126's five-attacker windows were answered by putting all five
    blockers on one 3/2 while two attackers marked `[menace — only a block by TWO OR MORE of
    your creatures counts; one creature alone does not block it at all]` went unblocked; five
    bodies bought 3 damage of 16, at 9 life and then at 5. The render is complete and
    explicit on BOTH the A-line and the B-line, and the guide's own heuristic — "give each
    attacker one blocker first, then put the leftovers on the biggest" — is ACTIVELY WRONG
    there: one blocker on a menace attacker is a wasted body AND stops nothing, so the
    heuristic manufactures the pile-up it was written to prevent. No guide in the pool had a
    menace rule at all. General form: where the render MARKS a case as requiring N of
    something, a heuristic written for the unmarked case names the marked case and scopes
    itself out of it, in the same breath, or it will be applied to it. Ship the all-or-
    nothing statement keyed to the rendered tag, and give the marked case its own line in
    the deciding section.

102. THIRD-FAILURE ROUTING: SHRINK THE RULE, AND MOVE THE CHECK ONTO THE PILOT'S OWN PLAN
    SENTENCE. #85 ends the guide lane at the second identical failure and routes to the
    render. This is what to do when the render is already CORRECT and complete — the case
    #85 does not cover. deck123's RULE 5 states in three separate paragraphs that the
    OPPONENT chooses which creature an edict takes; the option row prints the card text
    verbatim on the same screen; and for a third corpus the pilot cast the edict at five
    creatures and at three, and wrote a survival line naming the body it would remove. A
    fourth restatement has now been measured and is not the lever. Do two things instead:
    (a) DELETE one of the existing restatements so the rule gets SHORTER — length is itself a
    failure mode at 30-40 KB; and (b) re-point the check from the BOARD to the pilot's OWN
    PLAN SENTENCE, in the imperative, quoting the exact wrong sentences the corpus contains
    ("IF YOUR PLAN NAMES WHICH CREATURE AN EDICT WILL REMOVE, THE PLAN IS ALREADY WRONG").
    A plan-text check is self-applied at the moment of writing; a board check competes with
    everything else on a 25 KB screen. Then PREDICT THE PLAN-TEXT METRIC, not the outcome
    metric, so the next wave can tell which half moved — and record in the same edit that if
    the plan-text half fails too, the lane is exhausted and the remedy is an annotation on
    the row. Boundary: this is routing for the THIRD failure. A first failure is usually a
    missing fact and prose is right; a second is usually a contradiction elsewhere in the
    file (#96, #97). Only at the third, with the fact rendered, is restatement exhausted.

=====================================================================
EDITION AMENDMENTS — wave-48 (2026-08-27) — amendments 103-119
=====================================================================
Lessons from the wave-48 corpus review (fifth fair-hand corpus, `matchups-20260827-072004`,
binary eccf8284c: E1 + lanes N/O/P/Q). Each traces to a cited seat finding. Standing owner
doctrine (2026-08-26) governs every rule below: the REVIEWER owns the deck guide, synthesis
owns this skill and the general strategy, the core loop is the purpose; hard caps on the
model's legal choices are rejected; every guide rule is reasoned and odds-based, never a
code-like floor.

103. A GUIDE'S WHY MUST SURVIVE THE RENDER IT NAMES — DIFF EVERY QUOTED RENDER STRING AND
    EVERY QUOTED COST AGAINST THE CURRENT EMITTER, EVERY WAVE. deck123's RULE 1 justified a
    hard `M >= 50` ceiling with two sentences about the screen: "these windows routinely list
    exactly one action ... and no 'pass' row" and "at 1,541 creatures the attack screen handed
    this deck a 233,662 character prompt". Lane N put `0. Pass priority (take no action this
    window)` on 63/63 of those windows and lane O made the 257-creature attack screen 11,274
    chars; the pilot crossed the ceiling four times in one turn and paid none of the predicted
    cost (`seat-123-130.md`, P1/P2 FAIL, boundary B4 deleted). deck125's stack-line sentence
    ("the stack line and the counter row do not print [defender]") went false the same corpus
    when lane P shipped the tags (`seat-125-126.md` W36, W11). A guide that describes a screen
    the pilot will not see is a false sentence, and a false sentence costs trust on every true
    one — the trust doctrine runs in both directions. The check is mechanical: the review
    carry lists each lane's new strings; every wave, walk the guide's quoted render literals
    AND its quoted costs ("a 233,662-char prompt", "no pass row") against them. A rule whose
    WHY names a render the engine no longer produces is retired or re-justified in the same
    wave, never carried. This is #90's grep pointed at the WHY clauses instead of the keys, and
    #99's negative-existence sweep widened to "the render used to be X".
