    verbatim literal. The reply was `BLOCKS: B1:A3, B2:A4`: one blocker on each. **That answer does
    not contradict the affordance sentence; it never reaches it.** Restating an affordance the pilot
    never disputed is the #181 failure with the sign flipped; naming the wrong answer is what the
    evidence supports. (deck152 S4. The engine half — that both assignments were pruned and NO
    blocks were declared, with no re-ask — is an R-item and a HIGH, and the two are independent.)

226. **WHEN A LANE ADDS A *NUMBER* TO A CLAUSE A GUIDE RULE TREATS AS A BINARY FLAG, THE RULE IS
    REWRITTEN AS ARITHMETIC OVER THAT NUMBER IN THE SAME WAVE, AND A "FAIL" SCORED AGAINST THE OLD
    BINARY IS REPORTED AS *RULE STALENESS*, NOT A PILOT BREAK.** deck152's attack rule said "never
    for a creature whose tag contains even one entry reading `(you kill it, your attacker lives)`".
    This corpus the engine prints the price INSIDE that same parenthesis —
    `(you kill it, your attacker lives (blocking trigger: they gain 3, and their converter takes 3
    off you))` — which under a life-loop converter makes the surplus attack a wash rather than a
    gain. Scored against the old absolute the seat "failed" 3 windows / 8 A-lines; it won that game
    20 to -10 having never dropped below 20 life, on two unblockable fliers. The seat file must say
    which of the two it is BEFORE the number goes into a prediction table, because a staleness
    verdict and a break verdict point at opposite edits. Sibling of #187 (a shipped literal
    retires a derivation) and of #202. (deck152 S5.)

227. **AN EXCLUSION RULE STATES THE *RENDERED CLAUSE* THAT IDENTIFIES ITS MEMBERS; AN ENUMERATED
    CATEGORY IS ACCEPTABLE ONLY AS A GLOSS AFTER THE CLAUSE, NEVER AS THE KEY — BECAUSE A CATEGORY
    IS A SET THE PILOT CAN JOIN CARDS TO AND A ROW CLAUSE IS NOT.** deck162's RULE 2 brakes "draw
    engines" and then enumerates them (Howling Mine, Dictate, Puzzle Box, Forced Fruition, Master of
    the Feast). Under pressure the pilot widened the category to "anything I could cast before my
    punisher is out" and answered `Cast nothing right now` on **10 own-turn windows across two
    games** whose only spell was a Liliana's Caress or a Fog Bank — cards that hand the opponent
    nothing. Six of the ten are the same two-row menu on turns 4 to 8 of a game lost 0 to 38 in
    which the first punisher landed on turn 10. The engine had the discriminator on the row the
    whole time: every gift row prints `{feeds: the opponent draws N extra card(s) per turn;
    converters on your battlefield: K …}` and non-gift rows print no such clause. Re-keying to
    `{feeds:` makes the brake exact, keeps its two correct firings (Forced Fruition at K of 0) as a
    built-in control, and SHRINKS the rule. (deck162 S7; the mirror of #206 — closing a rule's empty
    case opened its exempt case one wave ago, and widening a category opened this one.)

228. **A GUIDE THAT CONTAINS BOTH A RESOURCE RULE (WHAT COUNTS TOWARD K) AND AN ORDERING RULE (WHAT
    GOES DOWN FIRST) IS READ AGAINST ITSELF EVERY WAVE: A CARD THE RESOURCE RULE COUNTS AS A
    PREREQUISITE CANNOT BE GATED BEHIND THE THING IT IS A PREREQUISITE FOR.** deck162's RULE 2
    counts Liliana's Caress toward K, and its cast order gated Caress behind "a Howling Mine,
    Dictate or Puzzle Box is on your battlefield" — so the card that makes a later engine's K read 1
    was ordered AFTER the engines it enables. The pilot obeyed the order and never cast it, in the
    two games that carried the deck's only windows. This check is a READ, not a corpus: it costs one
    pass and it caught a six-window loss here. (deck162 S8. Generalisation: any two rules that
    quantify over the same card set are read as a pair, in both directions.)

229. **A GUIDE WHOSE DECK HOLDS NO INSTANTS OR FLASH CARRIES ONE SENTENCE SAYING SO, KEYED TO THE
    ASK: "IF IT WERE CASTABLE THIS WINDOW IT WOULD BE A ROW."** Three of deck162's ten wrong declines
    carried an explicit "keep mana open for Underworld Dreams / Fate Unraveler / Ob Nixilis" on the
    seat's OWN main phase. Every one of those cards is sorcery speed. The pilot was importing a
    correct general habit into a deck that has nothing to hold mana FOR — and the surface already
    answers it, because a castable card is a row. Guides for decks that DO hold instants keep the
    habit and say nothing. **This is the shape to watch for: a per-deck fact that reads like a
    general one, which is exactly the kind that must be written down rather than assumed.**
    (deck162 S9.)

230. **AN ENGINE CLAIM BUILT BY JOINING `stderr` TO A TRANSLOG RECORD IS ANCHORED TO THE *WINDOW* —
    ITS OPTION COUNT AND ITS TURN BOUNDARY — NEVER TO A CARD NAME.** The seat that owns deck146
    filed its E-3 as a telemetry defect: `146v152` seq 63 records `choice: 5` /
    `chosen_text: "Cast nothing right now"` while `game-146v152-1788425074.stderr:2044-2070` shows
    Silverquill Command being cast, chosen (`chose 7 of 9`) and targeted — concluding that the
    record was wrong, that `latched_row_mismatch` had fired on bad fields, and that "everything
    downstream that reads `chosen_text`, this seat file's own take counts included, is affected".
    **Re-derived on disk, the join is wrong and the record is right.** Seq 63's menu has FIVE rows;
    the two stderr casting decisions in that block read `-> chose 3 of 4` and `-> chose 1 of 3`, and
    they sit between `Untap Phase ------------- Turn 14` (line 1993) and `Turn 15` (line 2162), five
    engine turns before seq 63's window. Seq 63's own line is at **3141**, `-> chose 5 of 5`, under
    `Turn 20`. The seat matched by card name across a game that casts that card more than once. The
    stamp is a TRUE positive exactly as the engine seat adjudicated it (the reply's header line
    `CHOICE: 3 (Cast Silverquill Command)` differs in index and name from the executed row, and the
    reply's own last coded line is `So, CHOICE: 5 (Cast nothing right now).`). Rule: a card name is
    not a key. Anchor on `options`/`options_text` length, on the turn banner above the block, and on
    the `-> chose N of M` arity — and when a seat file's conclusion would invalidate a whole class of
    fields, that is the claim synthesis re-derives first. (This step's own, forced by reconciliation;
    the #208 sibling for cross-source joins.)

231. **WHEN TWO SEATS PROPOSE COMPETING MECHANISMS FOR THE SAME SIGNAL, THE ADJUDICATION IS A
    CORRELATION ACROSS ALL GAMES, NOT A MATCHED PAIR — TWO POINTS FIT ANY HYPOTHESIS.** Three seats
    pinned the corpus's `dropping stale async answer` spike (63 -> **488**, +675%) to lane AA's
    interrupt-window stall floor; one seat argued instead that lane M's ask-cache replay tracks the
    drops "exactly", citing two games (`126v123` 172 replays / 64 drops; `152v130` 0 / 0) and
    recommending that AA be flipped LAST because it is "the RESCUER here, not the cause". Re-derived
    over all 21 games: **drops vs releases r = 0.9963** (drops equal releases exactly in 10 of 21
    games, mean absolute difference 1.14, and 434 of 488 drops fall within ±8 stderr lines of a
    release); **drops vs `chose to cast nothing` replays r = 0.5173**, and the pair that kills it is
    `125v123` (809 replays, 45 drops) against `162v130` (5 replays, 37 drops). The two-point fit was
    honest and wrong. Rule: a mechanism claim over a per-game signal is scored on every game in the
    corpus with the coefficient printed, and the citing seat names the games that would REFUTE it.
    (This step's own; the wave-53 analogue is #208, and this is its inferential half.)

232. **THE SIZE BAND IS RESTATED FROM THE MEASURED DISTRIBUTION EACH WAVE, AND THE DISCIPLINE IS A
    NET-CHANGE BUDGET PER WAVE, NOT AN ABSOLUTE CEILING.** #146's band was written against
    "27-38 KB" and has been stale by roughly a factor of two for several waves; wave-53's boundary
    finding B10 asked this step to restate it from measurement, and three wave-54 edit-texts quote
    three DIFFERENT bands from memory ("39.6-70.2 KB" twice, "39.6-74.7 KB" once), none of which
    matches the file sizes on disk. **Measured, on the deployed wave-54 guides: 41.4 / 55.3 / 58.6 /
    59.3 / 59.8 / 63.3 / 69.4 KB — the band is 40-70 KB, median 59 KB.** Net change this wave:
    deck123 +885 B, deck162 +1,730, deck146 +2,474, deck126 +2,724, deck152 +2,897, deck130 +3,103,
    deck125 +5,215 — **+19,028 bytes, +5.5% across the pool in one wave**, in a wave in which four
    of the seven seat files described their guides as at or near their ceilings and two named freeze
    candidates. An absolute ceiling is unenforceable against seven owners; a per-wave NET budget is
    checkable by one `stat`. Rule: every seat file states its guide's bytes before and after and its
    net change with the trims that paid for it (wave 53's B10, now honoured by five of seven);
    synthesis publishes the band and the pool's net change; **a guide whose predictions all passed
    that grows anyway is the #220 failure, and it is the only size finding that needs an argument.**
    (This step's own, discharging wave-53 B10.)

**Supporting instances recorded, not amended.** The `{feeds:` clause and its K-of-0 long form, the
`[named: <card>]` battlefield tag, the reveal chooser's `[does NOT qualify - goes to "put back"]` /
`[eligible for "choose a card"]` per-row verdicts, and the coexistence of `{modes live right now:}`
+ `[DRAW PRICE:]` + the menu-fit clause on one row (`146v162` s46 row 5) are four render surfaces
four different seats asked NOT to be changed — the #193 dedicated-line device working, recorded so
no later lane "simplifies" one off a row. deck126's mulligan (`126v162` s1: the odds-form one-land
branch firing on exactly the hand it was written for, the reply naming the cause the render
printed, the bottom sending the one redundant card, the game won 38-0) is the cleanest single
decision in the corpus and is #171/#203 working end to end. deck125's ceilings held on much smaller
denominators and are recorded WITH them per #217: sweeper at header 0 **0/40** (fifth corpus), land
drop **64/64**, `X = 3` **6/6**, low-X Revelation **0/51** (was 2/116 — #194's refusal-by-name
holding), counters on walls **0/22**, Lightmine below 3 attackers **0/59**. deck130's draw-punisher
rung is at **0 of 12**, a fourth corpus, and its face-damage floor at **1** break (6 -> 4 -> 1) —
both compressible in wave 56 on #200(c) if they hold again. deck146's `[DRAW PRICE:` declines
(**0 casts of 26 rows**) and deck162's second-copy Mine takes (**5, all at K >= 1**) are the two
render-to-behaviour results of the wave, and neither needed a guide sentence to happen — which is
#197's whole claim, now with two more instances.

---

# WAVE-55 AMENDMENTS (233-266)

Corpus `matchups-20260903-074354` (TWELFTH fair-hand corpus, 42 seat logs, 3,171 decisions, 21/21
natural), binary master **b228b8648** (wave-55 step-1 lanes A-E on base 8a1768d1c = wave-54 step-1 +
P purge + Q autotap + **R stall-floor hotfix**). Pilot `qwen36-35b-a3b` on Spark :8084. Every count
below was re-derived on disk by the synthesis step with python over the JSONL, **counting rows from
the rendered `prompt`**, never from the `options_text` array (#240). The wave-54 edition above is
byte-verbatim: the 1,186,215-byte prefix is `cmp`-verified.

## 233. A GUIDE THAT STATES AN EQUIVALENCE CHANGES NOTHING; ONLY AN IMPERATIVE MOVES A RATE — AND THIS CORPUS RAN THE EXPERIMENT ACROSS FIVE GUIDES AT ONCE.
*(This step's own, generalising deck125 S1. It is the strongest single result in the wave and it
governs every "the pilot ignores our clause" finding.)*

Wave-55 lane A gave the HOLD row **complete coverage**: 2,352 renders, LAST row on 2,352 of 2,352,
own-turn windows included, and in the 753 windows carrying `[you declined this exact list N times
already this turn]` at N >= 3 the row is present **753 / 753**. There is no window in the corpus
where the pilot *could not* stop the loop. Corpus-wide it was taken **67 of 753 = 8.9%**, which
three seats reported as a FAIL and two of them read as a render problem.

**It is not one rate. It is five, ordered exactly by what each deck's guide said**, measured on the
guides the corpus actually ran (wave-54 revisions + boundary pass), N >= 2 windows:

| deck | what its guide said about the row | windows | takes | rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **deck123** | names the row AND commands it: *"take that row at the FIRST dead window of the turn, not the fifth"* | 141 | **54** | **38.3%** |
| **deck130** | quotes the declined-note literal, no imperative on the row | 48 | 8 | 16.7% |
| **deck125** | names the row and calls it OPTIONAL: *"Take it or take 'Cast nothing right now' - **both are correct**"* | 381 | 25 | 6.6% |
| **deck126** | says nothing about the row | 155 | 1 | 0.6% |
| **deck146 + deck152 + deck162** | say nothing about the row | **190** | **0** | **0.0%** |

deck125 is the decisive cell. It is the deck with the MOST windows, its guide DOES name the row, and
it converts at one sixth of deck123's rate — because its sentence grants permission instead of
issuing an order. A guide that says "both are correct" has told the pilot the decision does not
matter, and the pilot then answers it the way it answers every other menu: from the row its guide
names elsewhere (`Cast nothing right now`, quoted 17 times in that file).

**Proposed rule.** A rule whose purpose is to CHANGE a behaviour is written as an imperative with a
trigger literal and a named wrong answer. "X is also correct", "X is safe", "you may take X", "both
are fine" are RECOGNITION text, and recognition text moves nothing: score it as an absent rule, not
as a failed one, and never file a render item against a class whose guide only recognises it.
**The audit is mechanical**: for every rule the seat expects to move a number, grep its own text for
`both`, `either`, `also correct`, `is safe`, `you may`, `it is fine to` — each hit is either
deleted or rewritten as an order with its wrong answer named.
**Limit.** This is not a licence for more text. deck123's imperative is TWO clauses, and deck123 is
the only guide in the pool that SHRANK this wave (-113 bytes).

## 234. EVERY "ANY ROW" ABSOLUTE CARRIES ITS EXCLUSION LIST INLINE.
*(Convergence: deck125 S4 + deck126 S9 — the same finding filed independently by both halves of one
seat pair, and it fired at deck126.)*

deck126 Rule #2: *"while both names are on your battlefield line, 'Cast nothing right now' is NEVER
your answer to a menu that prints any Cast row at all"*, while Rule #4 forbids a Tribute at
`at 0 this does nothing` and entry 7 forbids a `[second copy:` row. At `126v125` seq 169 and 185 the
only Cast rows WERE those two; the pilot obeyed the specific rules and broke the absolute. Three
windows later at seq 200 it obeyed the absolute and took the corpus's only `[second copy:` cast
(1 of 51 rows) at 3 life. A guide holding a universal in one section and its exceptions in another
is a guide with a live contradiction, and the pilot will resolve it differently in adjacent windows.
**Rule.** A universal and its exceptions live in the same paragraph. The check for an edition: for
every "always / never / any" sentence, list the rows another rule forbids and put them in that
sentence.

## 235. WHEN THE DECISION IS MADE ON A ROW, KEY THE RULE TO THE NUMBER THAT ROW PRINTS, IN THE ROW'S OWN WORDS AND POSITION.
*(deck123 S3.)* deck123 RULE 3 was keyed to the BATTLEFIELD line's `of which N are creatures`; the
row prints the same fact as `{right now: destroys 1 of their creature (...), 5 of yours}`. At
`123v152` s104 the pilot read the row, wrote a plan about *"saving my own 5 creatures"*, and did not
connect that 5 to a rule two screens above that forbids the cast at 4 or more. It cast a Damnation
that swept its own five-creature board and lost the game. Same shape twice more this corpus
(RULE 1's stop keyed to the battlefield `M` while the row prints `[repeat: you control M creatures]`,
23 renders; deck130's land plan keyed to a count of land rows while the line prints `... and N are
lands`). A rule keyed to a header the pilot must scroll back to is a rule with an extra step, and the
extra step is where the corpus shows it breaking.

## 236. WHEN A BREAK SURVIVES THREE PARAGRAPHS ACROSS THREE CORPORA, STOP WRITING GUIDE TEXT AND FILE THE RENDER ITEM — WITH THE SIBLING COMPARISON AS THE ARGUMENT.
*(deck123 S4.)* `Cast Lightning Greaves {2}` at `of which 0 are creatures` is now the FIFTH corpus.
The live guide attacks it in FOUR places and it broke again (`123v130` s11). Every sibling rung at
that seat that DID close closed when the ROW started carrying a verdict: the edict at N=0
(`at 0 this does nothing`) 1 -> **0 of 171 rows**; Tragic Slip on a dead row
(`kills 0 of the N legal targets`) **0 for three corpora**; the second Alarm 0 this corpus. The
Greaves row is the one class in that deck's menu that has never been priced. **Rule.** The seat file
states the comparison explicitly — which sibling rungs closed, and what closed them — because that
comparison IS the argument, and it pairs the filing with a prediction that names the exit ("if it
breaks a sixth time on a menu where this is the only cast row, the rung belongs to the render and no
further guide text is written for it").

## 237. A GATE WRITTEN ON A COUNT THE PILOT MUST CONVERT IS A PROXY; KEY IT TO THE PRINTED CONVERTED QUANTITY.
*(deck130 S9.)* deck130 gated Lay Waste cycling on a LAND COUNT — a proxy for "can I cast it this
turn" — and all four of the corpus's wrong cycles sit at the proxy's own boundary (two at THREE
lands, where the proxy says castable and the printed `Mana available:` said 3 against a {3}{R} cost;
two in one turn at five lands, a shape the count cannot express). **The tell that a proxy is failing
is a cluster of breaks at the proxy's boundary.** Where the engine prints the converted quantity
(`Mana available: N total`), key the rule to it; where it does not, say so and file the render ask.
Same family: creatures -> power, cards -> castable cards, lands -> mana.

## 238. A GUIDE MAY CITE A COUNT AS EVIDENCE FOR A RULE; IT MAY NOT STATE A COUNT AS A FACT ABOUT THE RENDER — AND AN "THE ENGINE NEVER OFFERS X" CLAIM SHIPS WITH ITS RE-VERIFICATION GREP AND ITS RETIREMENT TRIGGER.
*(Convergence: deck123 S1 + deck146 S-3.)*

deck130's wave-54 X rung carried *"across a whole corpus of twelve games it appeared ZERO times. Do
not wait for it"*. It was true when written and FALSE in this corpus: the marker rendered on **3 of
3** X menus, and at `130v146` s40 the pilot answered `X = 3` with the marker sitting on
`X = 1 {same kills as X=3, for 2 less mana}` two rows below — which is what a reader told not to wait
for the marker does. The mechanical check: grep the finished guide for a numeral adjacent to a render
string and for `zero times`, `never printed`, `not there`, `does not exist`; each hit is deleted or
made conditional (*"if no marker is printed, then ..."*).

**The permitted form is deck146's, and it is the pool's model.** Its guide asserts
*"the game NEVER offers you their land face"* about Emeria's Call / Agadeem's Awakening — an absence
claim, which this amendment would normally forbid — and it survives because it ships with (a) the
grep that re-verifies it (**re-checked by this step: 0 land-drop asks named either back face in
3,171 decisions; the only rows naming them are `Flip Side ... -> DISPLAY TOGGLE only`**), (b) the
primitive that explains it (`compare(isflipped)~equalto~1`, `borderline.txt:33968`), and (c) a
standing prediction (deck146 P10) whose whole purpose is to detect the day the engine is fixed, with
the instruction to delete the block in the same wave. **An absence claim with those three parts is
allowed; without them it is forbidden.**

**This amendment's own violation is already in the pool**: the seat that proposed it wrote
*"Last corpus every X menu this deck reached carried a marker - three of three"* into the deployed
deck130 guide (line 186). It is true today and it is the same shape. Boundary finding B4.

## 239. CLOSING A RENDER ITEM AND RE-KEYING THE GUIDE PARAGRAPH BUILT ON ITS ABSENCE ARE ONE PASS, AND THE REVIEWER WHO CLOSED IT IS THE ONE WHO KNOWS.
*(Convergence: deck123 S2 + deck130 G7.)* Three wave-54 render items closed at one seat pair this
corpus and each had a guide paragraph shaped around its absence: the X marker; fetch rows printing
no colour (now `and it adds {W} or {B} (you cannot make {W} right now)` on 60 rows, while the guide
still taught deriving the colour by hand); single-target `{kills:}` lists not marking ownership (now
`{kills whichever you target: THEIRS - ...; YOURS - ...}` on 71 rows, while the guide still warned
about rows that "name your own permanent" without naming the split that now distinguishes them). Each
replacement is SHORTER than what it replaced and strictly more mechanical. **Rule.** For every item a
reviewer marks closed, it states which guide paragraph was written against its absence and either
re-keys it to the new string or records explicitly that none depended on it. A closed render item
with no corresponding guide line is a reviewer who did not look.

## 240. COUNT ROW LITERALS FROM THE RENDERED `prompt`; THE `options_text` ARRAY IS A DIFFERENT OBJECT AND IT SILENTLY UNDER-REPORTS.
*(Convergence: deck125 S5 + seat-125-126 LOW #6; and it is the wave's second independent instance
after wave-55 lane D found three wave-54 docket numbers derived from the array that never rendered.)*
Lane D's discard verdicts and its `(copies k-m of n in your hand)` collapse render INSIDE the prompt
and are absent from `options_text`, which still holds bare card names. A first pass over the array
reported **0 renders for a feature that had shipped on 46 rows** — a shipped lane reported as
missing, which is a REVIEWER failure, not an engine one. **Rule for the audit procedure.** For any
literal that lives inside an option row, the denominator is a count of rows parsed out of the
rendered prompt text, and the seat file states which field it used. Where the two disagree, the
prompt is the pilot's world and the array is the engine's.

## 241. A PRIORITY ENTRY THAT CAN MATCH TWO ROWS AT ONCE NAMES ITS WINNER IN THE ENTRY.
*(deck126 S8.)* Rule #7 entry 1 ("Exquisite Blood or Sanguine Bond - whichever NAME is missing") ran
**9 takes of 9 windows** — a rule at its ceiling — and still produced a wrong answer, because at
`126v130` seq 14 BOTH were missing and both rows printed at the same price. The pilot took the
Blood; the guide's own Rule #3 says the Bond alone is a clock and the Blood alone does nothing you
can start. From t13 the pair sat out nine turns and the game went 23 -> 0. **The check for an
edition:** for every priority entry, ask "can two rows match this at the same time?" and, if yes,
name the winner in the entry. A perfect hit rate is not evidence that an entry is complete.

## 242. FOR A RULE INSIDE A PRIORITY LIST, THE DENOMINATOR IS WINDOWS WHERE NO HIGHER ENTRY MATCHED — AND THE SEAT REPORTS BOTH NUMBERS.
*(deck126 S10; the list-entry form of #216's `N raw / M live / K consequential`.)* deck126's Lantern
carve-out fired on 5 of 12 matching menus. Five of the seven declines took a HIGHER entry (four live
Idyllic Tutors, one Rule-7b Tribute) and are correct by the same guide. The real break rate is 2 of
12, and one of those was at 2 life where a wall is defensible. A raw hit rate on a list entry is a
fiction of the same family as wave-54's "raw 73, live 5".

## 243. "CAN THIS DECK EVER ACT HERE?" IS A GATE ON ADDING GUIDE TEXT FOR A WINDOW CLASS, ANSWERED FROM THE SEAT'S OWN CAST COUNTS BY PHASE BEFORE THE TEXT IS WRITTEN.
*(deck126 S11.)* deck126 was offered **169 opponent-turn windows across six games and made zero
casts in them**; its only instant is Tribute to Hunger and 218 of 228 Tribute rows read
`at 0 this does nothing`. Any edit adding opponent-turn instruction to that guide spends bytes on a
seam that has produced nothing in three corpora. The waste belongs to the RENDER layer, not the
guide — and note this amendment does NOT license the render layer to remove the windows (#doctrine:
hard caps on legal choices are rejected on sight); it licenses the guide to stay silent about them.

## 244. A MARKER ANSWERS "WHICH", NEVER "WHETHER" — AND A GUIDE TEACHING "THE MARKED ROW IS THE ANSWER" NAMES THE SCREEN WHERE "WHETHER" LIVES.
*(deck130 S8.)* At `130v146` s34 -> s36 the pilot reached the new
`[<- best trade: the most of THEIRS at the smallest cost to YOURS - at X=2 that is THEIRS:
Silverquill Silencer; YOURS: Goblin x2]`, took it, and quoted the marker's own words in its PLAN.
One of theirs for two of its own is a trade that deck's cast order forbids — and the marker is
CORRECT about what it says: it is the best row on that menu. The menu had no "cast nothing" row,
because that decision was one screen earlier. **The wording that carries this is a two-clause pair:
WHICH is decided here, WHETHER was decided at the row that opened this menu**, and the reviewer names
the screen where WHETHER lives. Generalises past X menus to every forced ask in the pool (target
menus, the London bottoming ask, the discard ask): a helper annotation inside a no-pass-row screen
can only rank the options it is printed on.

## 245. WHERE TWO OR MORE THRESHOLDS GATE THE SAME ACTION, THE GUIDE STATES THEM AS ONE WRITTEN LINE WITH ONE BLANK PER THRESHOLD, IN ONE PLACE.
*(deck130 S10.)* deck130 carried "at FIVE or more of their lands the spell is dead" in one section
and "at 8 life or less, stop destroying lands" in another. `130v152` s50 broke both at once — 7 life,
their board on SIX lands — and the reply shows the pilot holding exactly one of them in mind:
*"Land count is 6, which is >4, so land destruction is generally low value, but this is the only
playable card"*. It reasoned about the land floor, overrode it, and never mentioned the life floor.
A threshold the pilot does not have to write down is a threshold it can omit silently; the
write-it-down device (`Damnation: N <>, K <>, M <>`) is the pool's most reliably-obeyed construct —
deck123 wrote its three-number line on EVERY Damnation window this corpus — and it is cheap.

## 246. "THIS IS THE ONLY PLAYABLE CARD" IS A NAMED POOL-WIDE FAILURE MODE AND DESERVES ONE IDENTICALLY-WORDED PARAGRAPH IN EVERY GUIDE THAT HAS A HOLD RULE.
*(deck130 S11.)* The same sentence, in the model's own words, produced breaks at both seats of one
pair this corpus (`130v152` s50 *"this is the only playable card and it deals 2 damage to the
opponent as a bonus"*; `123v125` s83 *"dead, but only way to dig for Bloodline Keeper against counter
deck"*), and wave 54 recorded the identical shape at both. Both menus printed `Cast nothing right
now`. The failure is not about any card: it is a standing preference for action over the pass row,
and it survives every card-specific paragraph written against it. deck123's paragraph ("WHEN EVERY
CAST ROW ON THE MENU IS PRICED DEAD, ENTRY 8 IS THE PLAY, AND IT IS NOT INACTION") is in place and
that seat's dead casts went **5 -> 2 of 108 all-dead menus**; deck130 has no equivalent and took two
of its three worst casts under exactly that reasoning. **Recommendation: lift deck123's paragraph
verbatim into the guides that lack one rather than have each reviewer re-invent it** — and note it
is an imperative with its wrong answer named, which is why it works (#233).

## 247. ONCE PER DECK, RUN THE DECKLIST AGAINST THE PRIMITIVES FOR THE STRUCTURAL PROPERTIES THAT CREATE A DEAD SECOND COPY OR A DIVERGENT ATTACK LIST.
*(Convergence: deck123 S7 + deck130 S13.)* `130v146` s62 cast a second **Rorix Bladewing** at 14 life
off `[legendary: you already control Rorix Bladewing - legend rule: casting this sends one copy to
your graveyard (you choose which)]` — six mana for the identical board. Everything needed to predict
it existed before the corpus ran: `Res/ai/baka/deck130.txt` says `Rorix Bladewing *2` and
`mtg.txt:96836` says `type=Legendary Creature`. No reviewer had crossed those two files. The mirror
check matters as much: deck130's four Talismans DO stack (three separate `{T}:Add` lines,
`mtg.txt:117529`) and its `[second copy:` takes are correct 4 for 4.
The same pass covers the ATTACK-LIST divergence: `123v126` s53 had **37 creatures** on the
battlefield and **FOUR** rows on `Your creatures that can attack:`, because Intruder Alarm's
`doesnotuntap` (`mtg.txt:58850`) means only creatures made on a previous turn are ever available.
**The pass is mechanical over ~20 distinct cards**: `Legendary`, a non-stacking `lord(...)`, a
unique-effect enchantment, `doesnotuntap`, tap-as-a-cost on a token maker, a mass-untap trigger. Each
hit the deck runs 2+ of, or whose effect can split the creature count from the attack list, gets one
written line.

## 248. AN ORDERED PROSE RUNG OVER A NUMBERED MENU IS NOT EXECUTABLE: WRITE IT AS A NUMBERED SCAN WITH AN EXPLICIT ANTI-ANCHOR CLAUSE AND A COMPARISON STEP FOR ANY SUPERLATIVE.
*(deck146 S-1.)* deck146's cleanup-discard rung has been an ordered prose sentence for two waves. It
broke **2 of 7** in wave 54 and **2 of 7** again here, and the breaks share a shape the rung does not
address: **4 of the 7 answers begin `PUT: 1`**, and both wrong answers include row 1. The rung and
the pilot did not disagree about priority; the pilot answered from the top of the list. Three parts
the prose form lacks: (a) the rungs as a numbered list with "STOP at the first name you find";
(b) an explicit anti-anchor clause naming the failure ("do not answer from the top of the list, and
never answer `PUT: 1` because row 1 is first"); (c) for any tail rung saying "the priciest / biggest
/ highest", a COMPARISON step ("read the `{..}` cost off each row and compare the numbers"), because
a superlative over a menu is an operation, not a recognition (#224's sibling: #224 says name the
rendered field, this says state the operation over it).

## 249. AN ENUMERATING RENDER CLAUSE WITHOUT A QUANTIFIER IS NOT A COUNT, AND A GUIDE MAY NOT LEAN ON ONE FOR A COUNT.
*(deck146 S-2, with a render half routed to `general-strategy.md`.)* `146v123` s28 row 2 printed
`Cast Soul Shatter {2}{b} {right now: 24 tied at MV 0 (their highest): Human #1; Human #2; ... }`.
The primitive (`borderline.txt:106069`) is unambiguous: **one card**
(`sacrifice notaTarget(...manacost=convertedcost:highest...)`). The seat's plans at s24 and s28 both
read *"cast Soul Shatter to sacrifice all 24 Human tokens, wiping their board"*. The trust doctrine
says a printed clause must be believed — which makes the QUANTIFIER on an enumerating clause
load-bearing. **Guide side:** never derive a count from an enumeration whose clause does not state
how many objects the effect touches. **Render side:** any clause that lists N objects states how many
of them the effect touches, in the same clause.

## 250. THE TRUST DOCTRINE'S CONVERSE: A PRINTED ROW IS THE ENGINE'S ASSERTION THAT THE ACTION IS LEGAL RIGHT NOW, AND THE PLAN, THE LOG AND LAST TURN'S MEMORY ARE NOT EVIDENCE AGAINST IT.
*(deck152 S-1.)* `152v130` seq 34: the battlefield line said `4 are creatures, 4 of them able to
attack right now`; four A-lines printed, each `[no creature they control can block this attacker]`;
the header said `They have 0 untapped creatures able to block`. The reply held one back with
*"PLAN: ... Sigarda is already tapped."* Nothing was missing and nothing was false — the model
asserted a state the render had denied twice on the same screen. The doctrine as written is a
prohibition on teaching doubt; the gap is on the other side, and guides may reuse this sentence
verbatim: *"a row printed on this menu is the engine's statement that the action is legal right now;
the plan, the log and your memory of last turn are not evidence against it."* deck152 already
carried the plan-staleness rule for BLOCK tags and nobody had written it on the attackers side.

## 251. A MATCHUP POSTURE'S TRIGGER IS A NUMBER OR LITERAL ON THIS PROMPT; THE ARCHETYPE NAME IS PROSE AROUND IT.
*(deck152 S-2.)* deck152's posture section names archetypes (`vs REMOVAL/GRIND`, `vs AGGRO / GO-WIDE`,
`vs LIFEGAIN`, `vs A LIFE-TO-DAMAGE CONVERTER`) and only the last has a render key — and it is the
only one ever observed firing correctly. In `152v125` the seat lost **8 creature spells to
counterspells across 40 turns** with no posture to reach for, because "control deck" is not something
the render says. Postures were exempt from the existing category-re-key amendments; they are not.

## 252. A RE-KEY ONTO AN ENGINE LITERAL IS AUDITED FOR THE LITERAL'S COVERAGE OVER THE WINDOWS THE RULE FIRES IN, NOT ONLY FOR ITS RENDER COUNT.
*(deck152 S-3, recorded as method.)* The wave-54 boundary pass re-keyed deck152's attack rule onto
`They have N untapped creature(s) able to block`. Its precondition held — **90 of 90 attackers
records corpus-wide carry the header**, including all 62 at that seat pair, in both singular and
plural forms. A re-key onto a literal that renders 80% of the time is a rule with a silent hole, and
a render COUNT cannot detect that; only coverage over the rule's own window class can.

## 253. A BRAKE SHIPS WITH ITS RELEASE, READ OFF THE SAME SCREEN — OR STATES EXPLICITLY THAT NO RELEASE EXISTS.
*(deck162 S-1.)* deck162's K-of-0 brake is unconditional. Of its three violations this corpus **two
were correct plays and one was the break**, and the discriminator was on the prompt the whole time: a
punisher NAME on the `Your hand (N cards):` line. `162v123` s18 (Underworld Dreams in hand) produced
the `their next draw step draws 5 cards` forecast that won the game 20/0 five turns later; `162v125`
s98 (none in hand) is the break. **An unconditional brake turned the seat's two best engine casts of
the corpus into rule violations.** A brake without a release is a category ban, which is the exact
failure the same deck's previous re-key was written to fix one wave earlier.

## 254. A PROHIBITION ON A PLAN SENTENCE IS A PROHIBITION ON A PARAPHRASE CLASS: STATE THE STRUCTURAL TEST AND KEEP THE OBSERVED STRINGS AS THE RECEIPT.
*(deck162 S-2; the wave's strongest instance of the explicit-vs-adaptable trade, and it is measured.)*
deck162 banned "keep mana open" and "cast Underworld Dreams first". The residual is the same
behaviour under a THIRD sentence: *"cast Underworld Dreams or Fate Unraveler as soon as possible"*.
Enumerating observed strings has now failed twice in one deck: **10 windows -> 3 under an
enumeration, with the residual being a paraphrase the enumeration did not list.** Write the
structural test instead ("your plan names a card that is not one of the numbered rows; that card is
not competing for this mana"), keep the observed strings only as the WHAT THIS COST receipt, and
expect a fresh paraphrase next corpus.

## 255. WHEN A RULE'S DANGER LIVES IN A RELATION BETWEEN TWO PRINTED NUMBERS, WRITE THE RULE AS THE COMPARISON — A CONSTANT AGAINST ONE NUMBER CANNOT EXPRESS IT.
*(deck125 S2; extends #192's threshold-shape work with a preferred FORM.)* deck125's Revelation
carve-out read "your life is 5 or less AND the opponent battlefield header's second number is 1 or
more". At `125v146` seq 32 and 36 the seat was at **10** against three attackers whose printed powers
summed to **11**, with a life-gain row on the menu; it declined twice and died at -1. The number that
mattered (life vs incoming) was never on either side of the test. Preferred form: *"if <printed A> is
at or above <printed B>"*, falling back to a constant only when no second number is printed.
**Corollary routed to the render layer:** a relation the guide must compute from three P/T strings is
a relation the engine should print finished — this corpus has **50 non-blockers windows with
attackers declared against the seat and 0 carrying an incoming-damage total; 7 of the 50 were at or
past lethal**, all in the game that loss came from.

## 256. A GATE WHOSE EVERY OBSERVED VIOLATION WAS CORRECT IS MIS-SCOPED, NOT DISOBEYED: CARVE THE SHAPE OUT, DO NOT RESTATE THE RULE.
*(deck125 S3.)* deck125's tap-out gate has produced exactly three live breaks in two corpora and
**all three are a FIRST Staff of Nin at `casting this taps you out`** — one in wave 54 (unpunished)
and two here (`125v123` s49, `125v126` s49; both resolved, both pinged on the next upkeep, both games
won 32-0 and 44-0). The wave-54 response was to restate the gate harder. The right response is a
carve-out that keeps the rule's remaining scope explicit (second Staff, Elixir activation, Lightmine
Field), so it is a narrowing and not a repeal, with a two-sided falsifier: first-Staff takes N/N,
second-Staff takes 0.

## 257. WRITE THE HEAD OF A SEND-LIST AS A TIER AND THE TAIL AS A SEQUENCE.
*(deck125 S6.)* Four times this corpus the seat sent a LONE dead sweeper ahead of its counterspells
with the opponent header at 0 creatures (`125v152` s216, `125v162` s64, `125v123` s45, `125v126`
s166) — a send its seven-step list had no step for, and the right one every time. Meanwhile step 1
("Lightmine first") is 4 of 12 by the letter and every miss cost nothing because the alternative sent
was also dead. A strict sequence over items whose relative value is set by the BOARD, not by the
card, generates fake breaks at the top of the list and real gaps in the middle.

## 258. WHEN A LANE ADDS A CLAUSE INSIDE A STRING AN EXISTING RULE KEYS ON, THE RULE IS RE-READ AS THE COMPOSED STRING AND THE EDIT QUOTES THE COMPOSED STRING IN FULL.
*(deck126 S7; the composition-seam failure at the guide/render boundary rather than at a fragment
boundary.)* Blockers STEP 1 keys on `(your blocker dies, attacker lives)`. This corpus that
parenthesis grew a second clause INSIDE it: `may block A1 (your blocker dies, attacker lives
(blocking trigger: you gain 3 and may gain 2 more))`. Both halves are true; the new half prices the
block at 5 life and the old half prices it at one wall. At `126v146` seq 6 the seat blocked with both
walls at 20 life against a lone 1/1 [first strike, deathtouch], banked 7 life, lost Pride Guardian,
and five turns later met five attackers with one blocker and lost at -14. **This is the render
working as designed** — it is a guide item. The check is cheap: grep the corpus for the rule's quoted
literal and confirm it still occurs as a whole clause.

## 259. A LITERAL AUDIT'S THREE NUMBERS TEST PRESENCE, NOT TRUTH: A CLAUSE CARRYING A COMPUTED NUMBER IS VERIFIED AGAINST THE RECORD'S OWN FIELDS.
*(This step's own, forced by reconciliation 2 — and it is the sharpest silent-instrument instance
since the wave-54 X marker.)*

Wave-55 lane C shipped D16, "ability rows that point damage at a player print the life total". The
engine seat audited it and scored **PASS, 0 of 251**: every such row carries `they would be at N`.
The seat's own #188 audit reported old-renders 0 / new-renders 251 / takes 6 and moved on. Re-derived
against the records' own `opp_life` field: **238 of the 248 rows carrying `they would be at K`
compute K from a CONSTANT BASE OF 166**, at every real opponent life from 34 down to 1
(`2 damage -> at 164` on 176 rows, `1 damage -> at 165` on 61, one value, no variance). The 10
correct ones are TARGET-MENU player rows, a different emitter. Two seats scored the item PASS on
presence; one seat found the falsehood by reading a number.

**Rule.** Whenever an audited literal contains a number the engine computed, the audit's three
numbers gain a fourth column: **the number checked against the record's own field on the full
population where the field exists, or on a stated sample where it does not.** A missing metric, a
guard that never fires, and an absent bug all produce identical output; so do a correct clause and a
clause whose every value is wrong.

## 260. WHEN A LANE NARROWS A DOCKET ITEM'S SCOPE IN ITS OWN PREDICTION, THE LEDGER RECORDS BOTH PREDICTIONS AND THE NEXT WAVE SCORES BOTH — THE GAP BETWEEN THEM IS A NEW ITEM, NOT A FAIL.
*(This step's own, forced by reconciliation 4.)* Wave-54 docket D6 predicted "X menus rendering with
no marker: **0** (was 2 of 2)". Lane C shipped three ranked markers and wrote its OWN prediction as
"X menus **(kill-priced)** rendering with no marker: 0". This corpus: **14 X menus, 3 kill-priced —
all 3 marked (lane C PASSES in its stated scope) — and 11 monotone Sphinx's Revelation menus with no
marker of any kind, because none of the three marker families has a kill dimension to rank.** One
seat scored this FAIL 11/14 against the docket wording; another scored it UNTESTED because no X menu
reached its decks. Both readings are defensible and neither is the useful one. The ledger records the
docket prediction, the lane's scoped prediction, and — when they differ — the residual family as a
NEW ranked item with its own denominator.

## 261. BEFORE FILING A RENDER ITEM WHOSE EVIDENCE IS A REPEATED IDENTICAL ANSWER, GREP THE SEAT'S OWN GUIDE FOR THE IMPERATIVE THAT MANDATES IT.
*(This step's own, forced by reconciliation 5.)* The engine seat filed HIGH #3: on **6 of 6** Sphinx's
Revelation menus where a larger X was affordable (max X 6, 7, 8, 8, 8, 12) the pilot answered X = 3,
and on all five menus topping out at X <= 3 it took the max — a pattern so exact the seat read it as
a render vacuum (no marker, no fit clause, no collapse) and predicted a wave-56 experiment to settle
whether the anchor was in the guide. **The experiment is unnecessary and the answer is on disk**:
deck125's guide carries a section headed `=== SPHINX'S REVELATION - X IS ALWAYS 3 ===` which ends
*"reply with the OPTION number whose line reads 'X = 3'. Every time, and with no arithmetic in front
of it."* The deck seat scored the same behaviour **11/11 CORRECT** on the same records. This is a
guide rung executing perfectly, and the render item that survives it is a different, smaller one
(the monotone family carries no `{leaves N sources}` fit clause, so the only real trade-off — holding
up mana — is invisible). **Rule.** An engine seat that owns no deck files a render item on repeated
behaviour only after grepping the deck's guide for the rule; if a rule mandates the behaviour, the
finding is re-scoped to what the render still does not say and the guide half is named as the deck
seat's. Cost of the omission this wave: one HIGH rank and one wave-56 lane.

## 262. EXPLAIN A CORPUS-LEVEL METRIC SHIFT WITH THE WITHIN-CORPUS CONTROL IN WHICH THE RIVAL EXPLANATION PREDICTS THE OPPOSITE SIGN.
*(This step's own, forced by reconciliation 6; the method companion to #231's correlation rule.)*
Per-decision inference rose 23.9 s -> 26.1 s and the engine seat attributed it to server contention
using cross-corpus prompt-size bins plus concurrency arithmetic — strong, but every term is measured
across two different corpora. The decisive test is inside ONE corpus and it costs nothing: the games
were launched together at `-j 21` and finished over two hours, so concurrency falls monotonically
while each game's prompts GROW. Measured on the three longest games, first quartile -> last quartile:
`125v152` median latency **17.8 s -> 3.0 s** while the mean prompt went **12,622 -> 26,919 chars**;
`123v125` **24.5 -> 4.8 s** at 6,196 -> 16,431; `125v126` **20.7 -> 2.6 s** at 6,670 -> 17,847.
Latency falls six- to eightfold while prompt bytes double. Across all 21 games,
**corr(mean concurrency during the game, that game's median latency) = +0.82.**
**Rule.** Prefer the comparison in which the rival hypothesis predicts the opposite sign; report the
coefficient. **Consequence for the ledger** (carried into `engine-ledger.md`): per-decision inference
measured at fixed `-j` on a shared server is not an engine metric and must stop being carried as a
falsifiable engine prediction.

## 263. A TELEMETRY FIELD PRESENT ON 100% OF A RECORD KIND IS NOT AN ALARM, AND A STAMP'S SELECTIVITY IS REPORTED WITH IT.
*(Convergence: three seats independently — seat-engine-narration, seat-125-126 MED #4, seat-146-152-162
E-5.)* Lane E shipped `reveal_stall` / `reveal_stall_secs` / `reveal_stall_phase` to be "present only
when the driver was parked". Re-derived: the triple is on **12 of 12** reveal records;
`reveal_stall_secs` equals `latency_ms / 1000` to the second on all twelve (4, 5, 14, 24, 24, 42, 47,
55, 60, 148, 211, 474); `reveal_stall_phase` is **0** on all twelve; the poll-churn floor is
max(1,800 s, 3 x deadline) = 2,700 s and the largest value is 474. So it is a duration field that
duplicates a field the record already carries, and nothing selects the parked case it was built for.
**Rule.** Any new stamp reports, in the same wave it ships, the fraction of its record kind that
carries it. A signature on 100% of a kind and a signature on 0% of it are the same instrument: both
answer no question. Corollary already in force from wave 54: a lane whose change can alter any
emitted string, window or timing ships its disable flag in the same commit — and this wave adds that
**a disable flag that crashes is worse than no flag**, because the lane reads as A/B-able
(`WAGIC_GPT_BOARDINDEX=0` segfaults on this binary and on its base).

## 264. A STALE QUOTED LITERAL IS AN AUDIT DEBT; IT IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY A BEHAVIOUR FAILURE, BECAUSE THE PILOT FOLLOWS THE DESCRIPTION.
*(This step's own; a refinement of #209, forced by #233's table.)* #209 requires a guide to quote an
engine literal AS a literal, because the audit that keeps it true is a grep. This corpus shows what
that rule does and does not buy. deck123 and deck130 both quoted the **wave-54 HOLD row string, which
renders 0 times in this corpus** — and they are the two decks that took the row most (38.3% and
16.7% of N >= 2 windows). deck125 quoted a dead string too and converted at 6.6%; the four decks with
no sentence at all converted at 0.0-0.6%. **The literal is for the AUDITOR; the behaviour comes from
the surrounding description and its imperative.** So: a dead quotation is filed as an audit debt with
its wave and its correct replacement — it is NOT evidence that the rule failed, and it must never be
used to argue a rule should be deleted. The inverse error is the dangerous one and #238 covers it: a
guide asserting a clause does NOT exist goes false silently and the pilot acts on it.

## 265. WHERE THE CORPUS SHOWS A RUNG HELD, CHANGE THE SENTENCE'S REGISTER FROM REBUKE TO STANDARD, AND STATE THE ENGINE-SIDE RESIDUE AS NOT THE PILOT'S PROBLEM.
*(deck123 S5.)* `123v126` s57-s87 is 31 decisions in one Upkeep and `123v162` s36-s50 is fifteen in
one Draw step; across both, plus four Upkeep runs at `123v125`, the pilot cast **nothing**. Its
behaviour inside a known engine defect was correct at every window. A guide paragraph that rebukes it
("this deck took it LATE almost every time") spends its lines telling the model it is bad at
something it is now good at — and worse, a reader who is following the rule and still seeing the
window return has nowhere to go. The remedy is one clause naming the residue as engine-side ("the row
is not kept when a life total is ticking, and that is not your problem to solve; answer the SAME way
every time, and the one thing that must not happen is a cast"). This is not praise-writing: it is the
difference between a pilot reading a run of identical windows as evidence it has misplayed and one
reading it as noise.

## 266. A GUIDE NEEDS A SMALL MENU-LEVEL SECTION FOR FACTS ABOUT THE SHAPE OF THE LIST RATHER THAN ABOUT ANY CARD IN IT.
*(deck123 S6.)* `123v152` s104's menu carried `Cast Damnation {2}{b}{b}` and `Cast Damnation
{4}{b}{b} [from exile]` with byte-identical `{right now:}` verdicts; the pilot answered the dearer
one and swept its own board. Nothing in that guide said "prefer the cheaper row", because the
Damnation rule, the exile paragraph and the cast list are each written about ONE CARD and this is a
fact about a MENU. Three or four lines cover the class: two rows naming the same card, a row that is
a strict subset of another, the collapsed-run rule the X menu already has. deck130 has such a section
and it works (its `same kills as X=N` walk-down is 2 for 2 this corpus); deck123 did not, and the
missing line cost the game.

---

**Supporting instances recorded, not amended.** The wave-55 lane set produced five render surfaces
whose seats asked in writing that they NOT be changed, and they are recorded here so no later lane
"simplifies" one off a row: lane C's two-sided edict verdict with its commit clause
(`{right now: they control 1 creature - ... ; YOU control 1 creature - targeting yourself sacrifices
...}` on 151 windows, `{this row does not pick a target yet - taking it asks you next which of the N
legal targets above}` on 217, and the wave-54 model's unanswered prose question closed); lane C's
ownership split (`{kills whichever you target: THEIRS - ...; YOURS - ...}` 215 windows / 223 rows);
lane D's decode line for a multi-source block (123 windows) and its copy-tag collapse (123 windows),
which together took the wave-54 `#N` mega-menu class to **0 records with more than three rows of one
shape**; deck162's `DRAW FORECAST (theirs)` + `DRAW PUNISHERS on the battlefield` pair, off which
`162v123` s30 declared `ATTACK: none`, multiplied 5 x 3 against an opponent at 10, and won on their
draw step; and lane E's mulligan scope tail, which held on the only two windows it had (both KEEPS at
4 and 2 lands, ending a four-corpus break). deck123's edict rungs are at **0 of 171** rows reading
`they control 0 creatures - at 0 this does nothing` and **0 of 52** reading `- they choose which
one`, both #200(c)-compressible next wave if they hold. deck126's zero-Tribute rung is **0 of 218**
(was 0 of 99), its dead-tutor rung **0 of 18**, its reveal picks **5/5**, and every wave-54 prediction
that had a window PASSED — the second consecutive wave that guide has done so, and the case #220 was
written for.
